items.title: A l'entrada del tens clar
items.subtitle: At the coming of the bright season: troubadour round dance
items.source: Pierre Aubry, Trouvères et troubadours (Paris: Félix Alcan, 1909), pp. 60-61, from the chansonnier of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (Paris, BnF fr. 20050)

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Aubry, Trouvères et troubadours (1909), at p. 60
the same, p. 61 (the refrain and verses II-III)

items.blocked: Source check: compare with Aubry pp. 60-61, especially the first note of the refrain's second line (an F sharp: the head sits high, but its sharp is on the F space and the cadence G-F sharp-G wants it), the grace notes, and the second "E-ya!" (B, G, A, not B, c, d like the other two). Classroom check: the class as chorus (the "E-ya!" answers and the refrain), a soloist or the teacher on the verse lines, and a round dance in a circle.
items.notes: THE WORDS, verse I (sung): "A l'entrada del tems clar, - Eya, / Per joia recomençar, - Eya, / E per jelos irritar, - Eya, / Vol la regina mostrar / Qu'el es si amorosa. / Alavi', alavia, jelos, / Laissaz nos, laissaz nos / Ballar entre nos, entre nos." At the coming of the bright season, to begin the joy again and to annoy the jealous, the queen wants to show that she is so full of love. Away, away, jealous ones, let us, let us dance among ourselves.
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with Aubry's readings of the refrain's F sharp and the second "E-ya!" marked as guesses, an underlay typo fixed ("je_ los" to "je_ los", so "los" falls on the F sharp), verses II and III as text, and no tuning; keep correcting here

dossier.function: A round dance for the coming of spring: the "April queen" calls everyone, girl and boy, to come and dance, to spite the jealous old king; the chorus shouts "Eya!" after each of the soloist's lines and sings the refrain, "Away, away, jealous ones, let us dance among ourselves."
dossier.elements: Call and answer: a soloist's line (always the same seven notes, B c d d d B A) and the chorus's "E-ya!" held over four bars; then a sixteen-bar refrain for everyone. 3/4 in a long-short swing (half then quarter), the medieval first rhythmic mode as Aubry read it; G is the final, the range an octave (F sharp to e).
dossier.practice: Vif (Aubry). A soloist and a chorus, as the plate marks them; danced in a ring. The band plays only a tabor-like drum (ours); the plate has the voice alone.
dossier.honesty: Anonymous, 12th-13th century, from the chansonnier of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (Paris, BnF fr. 20050), which writes no rhythm; the 3/4 long-short rhythm, the grace notes and the two F sharps are Aubry's reading (1909). The drum is ours.
dossier.licence: Pierre Aubry (1874-1910), Trouvères et troubadours (Paris: Félix Alcan, 1909): public domain in the US, Canada and Europe (Aubry d. 1910).
dossier.respect: A secular spring dance; the "jealous" are the old husband and his kind, a stock figure of the genre. Nothing sacred.
dossier.review: An early-music singer, for the Occitan words and the rhythm.
dossier.accompaniment: Aubry prints the voice alone; the tabor-like drum is ours, bass and chords rest. Style folk only as a nominal setting, since the band lines decide what plays (conservative guess, 11 November 2026)
dossier.lyrics: Occitan, three verses with the refrain; verse I under the notes, II and III as text with an English meaning. All fit for class; the jealous old king is a stock figure of the genre (conservative guess, 11 November 2026)

items.title: Adana melody
items.subtitle: Peasant melody from Adana: hearing a neutral second
items.source: Raouf Yekta Bey, "La musique turque", Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (1922), p. 2951

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (1922), p. 2951 (Raouf Yekta Bey, "La musique turque")

performanceNotes: No recording possible for this exact melody: Yekta gives no title and says its author is unknown. For the sound of the mode, any taksim or folk song in makam Uşşak; for the region, the Çukurova folk tradition of Adana (bağlama, davul and zurna). Listen and choose one before linking.
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Yekta p. 2951 (the dotted sixteenth and thirty-second figures, and the natural on G in bar 7); confirm the page of the Sofyan rhythm (Yekta's usul chapter, "I. Rythme Sofian"). A Turkish musician to hear the tuning (B about 20 cents flat) and say which makam it is (Uşşak or Hüseyni). Classroom check: play it tuned and then in plain equal temperament, and ask the class which B is "the right one".
items.notes: YEKTA'S TETRACHORD (p. 2951): "Valeurs justes": la to si 65536/59049, si to do 2048/2187 (i.e. 2187/2048 up), do to ré 9/8 (the whole fourth 3/4, i.e. 4/3 up). "Valeurs approximatives": 10/9, 16/15, 9/8. Compare his second example on the same page, a Turkish tune "essentially in A minor", built on a pentachord A B C D E with B a full tone above A (9/8).
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with Yekta's own tuning (the %%tuning line already here) and a persian style under the record's Sofyan band lines; bar 7's last two notes (G natural, F sharp) kept as read and named as uncertain in an N: line; keep correcting here

dossier.function: A "simple popular melody collected in Asia Minor, among the peasants of the province of Adana"; Yekta prints it to show that a melody a European would call A minor without a leading tone is in fact in another mode, built on the tetrachord A-B-C-D with a B lower than the European one, and that "even a man who knows nothing of music" in the East hears the difference (p. 2951).
dossier.elements: 2/4, quarter = 56; eight bars, the first two repeated; dotted sixteenth and thirty-second figures (a "snap") on almost every beat; final A, range F sharp to e; the tetrachord A B C D with E above and G, F sharp below as ornaments.
dossier.practice: Unhurried. No words were printed: play it on the recorder or hum it. The point is the B: Yekta gives its exact place.
dossier.accompaniment: Yekta prints no accompaniment for this melody. Turkish rhythmic cycles (usul) are played on a drum with two strokes, düm (low, the right hand at the centre) and tek (high, at the rim); his first usul, Sofyan, in two beats, is "düm - tek ka" (a dactyl: a long and two shorts). Band here: Sofyan on the kick (düm) and rim (tek, ka), our choice of usul for a two-beat folk melody, not Yekta's for this tune; no bass, no chords. Folk practice in Adana (Çukurova) would use bağlama, or davul and zurna; needs a bağlama sound.
dossier.lyrics: None printed.
dossier.honesty: The melody as Yekta printed it. The tuning line is built from his own ratios for the tetrachord (A to B 65536/59049, B to C 2187/2048, C to D 9/8: B at 180.45 cents above A, C at 294.13, D at 498.04); E is taken as the pure fifth 3/2 above A; the other notes stay in equal temperament. The Sofyan drum is ours.
dossier.licence: Raouf Yekta Bey (1871-1935), "La musique turque", in Lavignac and La Laurencie (eds.), Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (Paris: Delagrave, 1922): public domain in the US (1922) and in Canada (Yekta d. 1935).
dossier.respect: A secular folk melody; nothing sensitive. Yekta wrote as a Turkish theorist answering European dismissals of Eastern scales; his own argument is the lesson.
dossier.review: A Turkish musician (a bağlama or ney player), for the makam and the tuning.

items.title: Aloha ʻOe
items.subtitle: Farewell to Thee
items.source: Queen Liliʻuokalani, Aloha Oe: Farewell to Thee, autographed sheet music placed in the Liliʻuokalani School cornerstone, 12 April 1912, Hawaiʻi State Archives M494-3-2, vocal score pp. 3-4; public domain

sourceUrls.label: Hawaiʻi State Archives exhibition identifying the Queen's manuscript collections and the 1912 autographed Aloha ʻOe score
Hawaiʻi State Archives, M494-3-2, seven-page scan of the autographed 1912 score
University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa catalogue record SCORE AL 008 and historical note
Library of Congress National Recording Registry essay on the song's history and later reception

performanceNotes: This record was read from the Queen's autographed score, not from a modern recording. A reviewer-led demonstration should establish Hawaiian pronunciation and the relationship between solo verse and communal refrain; do not copy a commercial recording's arrangement.
items.blocked: The autograph score and authorship are checked, but no human review has occurred. A Native Hawaiian music educator or historian, a competent Hawaiian-language speaker, a second score reader and a classroom music teacher must check the text, pronunciation, historical framing, verse-to-chorus practice and classroom key before publication.
items.notes: CONTEXT: Hawaiʻi State Archives dates the composition to 1878; the University of Hawaiʻi catalogue says it was written in 1877 or 1878 and later transcribed during the Queen's 1895-1896 house arrest. The 1912 edition credits both words and music to "Her Majesty Liliuokalani of Hawaii" and prints the 1884 copyright notice. These are authored historical facts, not evidence that every later tourist arrangement reflects Hawaiian practice.

dossier.function: Queen Liliʻuokalani's composed Hawaiian farewell and love song; in class it can teach solo verse and communal refrain, sustained phrase singing, a one-beat pickup and the chromatic upper neighbour G-sharp
dossier.elements: sixteen complete 4/4 bars after a one-beat pickup; G major, D4-C5 range, mostly stepwise verse and refrain, dotted-quarter/eighth figures, a held verse cadence that leads directly into the refrain pickup, and two written G-sharps that resolve to A
dossier.practice: The 1912 score marks Moderato, gives the verse to a solo voice with piano and expands the refrain to SATB chorus with piano. Quarter note = 84 is our rehearsal estimate, not the Queen's metronome mark. Let one singer or a small group carry the verse and the class join on the refrain. The written G-major range D4-C5 fits the conservative C4-D5 young-unison range, so G is the first rehearsal key to test
dossier.accompaniment: The source documents composed piano accompaniment and SATB writing for the refrain, but this workshop record transcribes only the vocal melody. Begin unaccompanied or with a quiet pitch reference; do not add ukulele, steel guitar, hula percussion or a generic "island" groove as though the score required it. Any generated harmony must be labelled as a new classroom arrangement, not traditional Hawaiian practice
dossier.lyrics: The autograph prints Hawaiian text in 1912 orthography without modern ʻokina or kahakō, plus English and German singing translations. This ABC keeps the plate's Hawaiian spelling and the refrain's printed English phrases as source evidence. A competent Hawaiian-language speaker must supply modern orthography, meaning and pronunciation before students sing it
dossier.honesty: Authored historical-source transcription, not an anonymous folk song: words and music are by Queen Liliʻuokalani, composed in 1877 or 1878. The melody follows the 1912 autographed edition at Hawaiʻi State Archives; ABC spelling, bar numbering, rehearsal tempo, melody-only reduction and muted-band directives are ours
dossier.licence: The composition and 1884 publication are public domain; Liliʻuokalani died in 1917. Hawaiʻi State Archives provides the 1912 autographed score as an open government archive scan. Reuse this melody transcription as public-domain source material, while separately crediting the Queen and the archive
dossier.respect: Name Queen Liliʻuokalani and the Hawaiian Kingdom context. University of Hawaiʻi notes that the song can be heard both as a love song and as a statement of Hawaiian sovereignty. Do not reduce it to tourist "island music," label it traditional or anonymous, stage a generic hula, or detach it from the overthrow and annexation history when that history is discussed
dossier.review: Native Hawaiian music educator or historian, competent Hawaiian-language speaker, second score reader and classroom music teacher; all reviews still required

items.title: Arirang
items.subtitle: Korean folk song, as Hulbert wrote it down in 1896
items.source: Homer B. Hulbert, "Korean Vocal Music", The Korean Repository 3 (Seoul: Trilingual Press, February 1896), p. 51; archive.org, University of Illinois copy

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Korean Repository vol. 3 (1896); the article is pp. 45-53 (may not be the Illinois copy the notes name)

items.blocked: Confirm bar 2's rhythm (the print shows no flags; read as quavers to match bar 1 and fill the bar), and have a Korean culture bearer hear it with the janggu.
items.notes: The oldest written Arirang. Hulbert's romanisation is kept (A-ra-rung for Arirang); in today's spelling the words are "Arirang arirang arariyo, arirang eolsa bae ddiwora. Mungyeong saejae bakdal namu, hongdukkae bangmang-i da naganda": the birch trees of Mungyeong pass all go to make washing clubs. Bar 2 has no flags in the print; it is read as bar 1 (two quavers and a minim), which fills the bar.
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with Hulbert's romanised words and a modern spelling in an N: line; bar 2's rhythm guessed as bar 1 (two quavers and a minim) and named; korean style, equal temperament; keep correcting here

dossier.function: folk song (minyo); the "Mungyeong Saejae" Arirang, which Hulbert heard everywhere in Seoul in 1896; the chorus is fixed and the verses are improvised
dossier.elements: 3/4 (Hulbert's notation of a lilting triple metre, the semachi jangdan); five notes, G A C D E, ending on G; the chorus "Arirang, arirang, arariyo" then a verse about the birch trees of Mungyeong Saejae made into washing clubs
dossier.practice: moderate and swaying; a singer leads the verse and everyone sings the chorus; the janggu drum keeps the jangdan; the band holds an open fifth on G with a janggu-like pattern on the kick and rim
dossier.honesty: arranged: the melody and Hulbert's romanised words as he printed them; the drone and drum pattern are ours, after the semachi jangdan as commonly taught
dossier.licence: public domain (Homer B. Hulbert, "Korean Vocal Music", The Korean Repository 3, February 1896, pp. 45-53; Hulbert died 1949); read bar by bar from the archive.org scan of the University of Illinois copy on 2026-11-10
dossier.respect: Arirang is a national song of Korea, North and South, and on UNESCO's list (2012, 2014); present it as a living song with many regional versions, this one as the earliest written down, by an American missionary
dossier.review: a Korean culture bearer or a teacher of gugak before publishing
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: the janggu (hourglass drum) keeps the jangdan under the singer; Hulbert prints the melody only (conservative guess, 11 November 2026). Band here: the korean style, a janggu-like pattern on kick and rim in three with an open fifth on G.
dossier.lyrics: Hulbert's romanised chorus and one verse (the birch trees of Mungyeong Saejae made into washing clubs), kept under the notes, with a modern spelling in the N: line; fit for class; not yet checked by a Korean speaker (conservative guess, 11 November 2026).

items.title: Ba ban (八板)
items.subtitle: Eight Beats: China's best-known instrumental tune
items.source: Mary Martin Richard, Paper on Chinese Music (Shanghai, 1899), Appendix D, "Popular Airs", No. 20 "Ba Ban", p. 33

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Mary Richard, Paper on Chinese Music (Shanghai, 1899), Appendix D, No. 20 "Ba Ban", p. 33
the same, around p. 24: Richard on Ba Ban as the best-known tune in China

performances.label: "Lao liu ban", a Jiangnan sizhu ensemble (title checked, not yet listened to): the best-known descendant of Ba ban

performanceNotes: Ba ban (Eight Beats) is the "mother tune" of a whole family: Lao ba ban in the north, Lao liu ban and its slower variations (Zhonghua liu ban, Man liu ban) in Jiangnan sizhu (silk-and-bamboo) music; recordings of these are plentiful; choose one by a named ensemble.
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Richard p. 33, No. 20 (a broken barline in the last line, read as a barline: "A c | A G | F2"). Listen to a Lao liu ban / Lao ba ban performance and say how close Richard's version is. Classroom check: on recorders, in four sections, then the whole, with the teacher ornamenting a second line (heterophony) once the band can play one.
items.notes: THE PLATE: 2/4, no key signature (written here in F, since the tune is pentatonic on F and no B occurs), three staves of quarters and halves, double bar at the end of the first staff and of the piece; headed '"Ba Ban"   Popular Airs.'
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with the broken barline in the last section read as a barline (bars 39-40) and named; instrumental; folk style under the record's band lines (wood block only), equal temperament; keep correcting here

dossier.function: An instrumental popular air: Richard (1899) calls it a tune known all over China, by more people than any other single tune. It is played, not sung, and is the framework that ensembles vary and ornament.
dossier.elements: 2/4 in quarters and halves; pentatonic on F (F G A c d, the gong mode), ending on F; range C to f; three phrases (16, 12 and 13 bars), each answering the last with the same falling cadences (F2 | C D | F2).
dossier.practice: Played by an ensemble in heterophony: everyone plays the same tune, each instrument filling it out in its own way (passing notes, octaves, repeated notes; in Chinese, jiahua, "adding flowers"). In class: learn the skeleton on recorders in sections, then let some players add notes between the beats while others keep the plain line.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: a silk-and-bamboo (sizhu) or wind-and-percussion ensemble, all on the melody: erhu (two-string fiddle), dizi (flute), pipa (lute), yangqin (dulcimer), sheng (mouth organ), with a clapper (ban) marking the downbeat; never chords. Band here: only a wood block on the first beat of each bar, standing in for the ban; no bass, no chords. Needs: a heterophony part (the tune on a second sound, ornamented), and erhu, dizi, pipa, yangqin sounds.
dossier.lyrics: None: an instrumental piece.
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the melody as Richard printed it, in her appendix of popular airs. Her version is longer than the usual 68-beat Ba ban (82 beats here); it is printed as she heard it, and the record does not claim it is the standard form. The wood block is ours.
dossier.licence: Mary Martin Richard (d. 1903), Paper on Chinese Music (Shanghai: American Presbyterian Mission Press, 1899): public domain everywhere.
dossier.respect: Avoid the first part of the same appendix (Nos. 1-17), Confucian ritual hymns. Richard was a missionary; some of her appendix tunes were adapted for hymns. Ba ban itself is a secular popular tune.
dossier.review: A player of Chinese instruments (Jiangnan sizhu), for the form and the ornaments.

items.title: Black Hills Powwow song (fragment)
items.subtitle: A phrase of a Northern powwow song: lead and seconds over the drum
items.source: Clip 13 of a Dust-to-Digital Instagram post (19 October 2026), filmed by Jenn Nicoteen at the Black Hills Powwow; draft by pitch tracking

sourceUrls.label: Dust-to-Digital on Instagram (posted 19 October 2026), clip 13 of 20: the Black Hills Powwow, Rapid City, South Dakota, via Jenn Nicoteen on Facebook

performances.label: the Black Hills Powwow, Rapid City, South Dakota (Dust-to-Digital, October 2026; filmed by Jenn Nicoteen, shown on "Jenn's Reels")

performanceNotes: The clip is 17 seconds of an indoor arena: jingle-dress and fancy-shawl dancers in a circle; the drum and singers are heard but not seen. Jenn Nicoteen's Facebook reel is the original; the full song, and the drum's name, may be there.
items.blocked: Source check: name the song and the drum group singing it, and ask the group (or the powwow committee) whether it may be taught; until then nothing here is used in class. Transcription: a machine draft of the 17 seconds (the lead's phrase, the seconds' answer down to the low F, the start of the next push-up), sung with wide slides under crowd noise and jingles; it needs a powwow singer's ear, and ideally a longer, cleaner recording of the same song.
items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): the clip's sustained part (harmonic/percussive separation, which takes out the drum strokes and the jingles) was pitch-tracked between G3 and E6; the singing sits about 40 cents above A=440 at the start and sags 20-30 cents by the long F, which is taken as the tonic (7.9-9.4 s, with the octave below). Phrases: the lead 0.2-4.7 s (B to C6, then B, A, G, A, B flat, A, a dip to C5, A held), the seconds 5.6-9.4 s (F sharp, B, E flat, E, F held), the next phrase 9.5-13.4 s (a quick turn G, F sharp, B, F sharp, then E, B4, G, D, G, A, F, A, B flat 4, A flat 4), drum only 13.5-15.7 s, and the start of the next (F sharp, 15.8 s). One eighth here is one drum stroke (about 0.30 s). Scored against the pitch track, each phrase aligned at its own start: 53% of voiced frames in all (lead 53%, seconds 64%, the third phrase 34%), lower than a steady instrument would give because of the slides.
items.kindNote: Seventeen seconds: the lead's opening phrase, the answer down to the tonic, and the start of the next phrase, drafted by pitch tracker; missing: the song's name and owners, the vocables, the rest of the form (the four push-ups, honor beats, tail), the drum part as played, and the dance it was sung for.

dossier.function: A powwow song sung at the drum for the dancers in the arena; this one carries jingle-dress and fancy-shawl dancers, so most likely an intertribal or a women's category song. Powwow songs are made and owned by singers and drum groups; some are ceremonial (honor songs, flag songs, veterans' songs) and are not to be sung outside their place.
dossier.elements: Northern style as heard: a high, strained lead that enters near the top of the voice (C6) and falls in terraces; the seconds answer from F sharp down through E flat and E to a long F, sung with the men an octave below; a new phrase then starts high again (G and B) and falls to A flat 4 below the tonic. The notes heard are F, G, A, B flat, C with B natural, E flat, E and A flat as slides and passing notes; every note is approached by a slide.
dossier.practice: Very loud, high and bright; the drum is struck together by several singers seated round one large drum, a steady beat of roughly 200 strokes a minute in this reading (unsteady under the crowd). The song falls from the lead's opening down to the low tonic; the whole song is repeated four times ("push-ups"), with honor beats (accented strokes) in places.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: one large bass drum played by the singers themselves, nothing else. The band plays nothing here; if the class ever uses this, one floor drum with soft beaters, played together.
dossier.lyrics: Not taken: the words were not audible, and powwow songs are often sung in vocables or in a Native language. None to be sung without the owners' consent.
dossier.honesty: Traditional practice; the song itself is probably owned. This draft is ours: the pitches were read by pitch tracker from a crowd recording, the slides reduced to single notes, and the lengths and bar lines guessed. Not a reliable transcription.
dossier.licence: Unknown: the song may be the composition of a living singer or drum group. The recording belongs to Jenn Nicoteen and the powwow; only an outline of the melody was taken, and no audio or video is kept here.
dossier.respect: Ask before teaching. Powwow singing belongs to Native communities and to the drum groups who make the songs; some songs are ceremonial. Present it only with the community's permission, name the drum and the powwow, and do not imitate the singing style as a novelty. If the song is one the singers say may be shared, a Lakota or Northern Plains singer should teach it.
dossier.review: A powwow singer or the drum group itself; the Black Hills Powwow committee (Rapid City), for the song's name and whether it may be taught.

items.title: B'qāw ʿala khēr
items.subtitle: Stay well: the Maghreb's closing song
items.source: Jules Rouanet, "La musique arabe dans le Maghreb", Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (1922), p. 2824

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (1922), p. 2824 (Rouanet, "La musique arabe dans le Maghreb")

performanceNotes: No recording found yet; the same places as Rāna jīnāk (AMAR; the Yafil 78s on Gallica). Listen before linking.
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Rouanet p. 2824, especially the naturals (E natural only where he marks one; the other E's are E flat by the key signature), the three half-bars of 3/8 he prints inside the 6/8, and the return to the sign. An Arabic speaker for the words. Classroom check: as the goodbye song, with a couplet for each child, as the tradition names each guest.
items.notes: THE PLATE: "M.M. dotted quarter = 108", 6/8, two flats, a sign (segno) after the pickup and a return to it at the end; three staves with words "B'kaou aâ la kheir! neb-ghi ne-rou-oua h' H'ass el moued-den fes-sa-ma-i ci Ah! Eb-kaou aâ la kheir!". Below, "Rythme d'accompagnement" in two lines of alternating eighths.
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with Rouanet's transliterated words under the notes and their English meaning in an N: line; the approximate underlay of "fes-sa-ma-i ci Ah!" and the signature E flats kept as read and named in the N: line; equal temperament (no documented tuning); persian style under the record's band lines; keep correcting here

dossier.function: The closing song of every Maghreb feast: the musicians' leave-taking of the hosts who listened to them (Rouanet's footnote 2), "the obligatory conclusion of every feast, whatever its character, where there is any music at all". Every couplet begins "Stay in peace!"; when the traditional couplets run out, the singers improvise lines naming the guests and the people they wish to honour, rhyming the names with formulas of thanks.
dossier.elements: 6/8, dotted quarter = 108; a two-eighth pickup and three short phrases, ending on B flat and going back to the sign; key of two flats with E natural as a leading tone to F; range B flat to g.
dossier.practice: Sung by the musicians as they leave, the drums keeping the alternating rhythm. In class: the goodbye song at the end of a lesson, the first line sung by all, then couplets with each child's name, the way the singers name each guest.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition (Rouanet pp. 2823-2824, 2838): the feast's musicians, indoors the women's ensemble with kamanja (violin), tar (jingled frame drum) and derbouka (goblet drum); outdoors ghaita with drums. Rouanet's printed "rythme d'accompagnement" alternates a high stroke and a low stroke by eighths: high on 1, 3 and 5, low on 2, 4 and 6 of the 6/8 bar. Band here: high on rim, low on bd, his rhythm exactly; barred in 3/8, the pattern alternates bar by bar. No bass or chords. Needs: derbouka, tar, kamanja.
dossier.lyrics: Rouanet prints the first couplet: "B'kaou aâ la kheir! nebghi nerououah', h'ass el moueddén fes-samai ... Ah! Ebkaou aâ la kheir!": tentatively بقاو على خير، نبغي نروّح، حسّ المؤذّن في السما, "Stay well! I want to go home: the muezzin's voice is in the sky (it is dawn) ... Ah! Stay well!" Fit for class; the muezzin line marks the hour the feast ends. The class couplets with names are the tradition's own practice (footnote 2). The Arabic script and translation wait for an Arabic speaker.
dossier.honesty: Traditional, anonymous; notes, words and rhythm as Rouanet printed them (1920), barred here in 3/8 (his 6/8 bars are pairs of these) so that the three half-bars he prints need no change of metre; the small notes before his sign are the pickup, written here once at the start.
dossier.licence: Jules Rouanet (1858-1944), in Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (Paris: Delagrave, 1922; section copyright 1920): public domain in the US and in Canada (Rouanet d. 1944).
dossier.respect: The words mention the muezzin's call, as the sign that night is over; nothing in the song is a religious text. Rouanet's framing is a colonial scholar's; the record keeps his facts about the music.
dossier.review: An Arabic speaker familiar with Algerian song, for the words and the class couplets.

items.title: Bújj, bújj, zöld ág
items.subtitle: Crawl through, green branch: Hungarian arch game
items.source: Kiss Áron, Magyar gyermekjáték-gyűjtemény (Budapest, 1891), Újhold-játék No. 4, p. 207

sourceUrls.label: Hungarian Electronic Library (MEK): Kiss Áron, Magyar gyermekjáték-gyűjtemény (1891), reprint of the 1891 pages; this game at printed p. 207 (PDF p. 235), Nos. 3 and 4, with the game on p. 206

performanceNotes: The Institute for Musicology in Budapest holds many field recordings of "Bújj, bújj, zöld ág" (for example Szebény, Baranya county, 1965, collected by Andrásfalvy and Olsvai; zti.hungaricana.hu). It is still one of the best-known Hungarian children's games, so school and kindergarten recordings are easy to find; listen and choose one sung by children before linking.
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Kiss p. 207, No. 4 (bar 7 "zöld le-ve-": G, G, E). A Hungarian speaker for the words and the translation. Classroom check: the arch game as Kiss describes it, with the "raj-ta" bars sung once for each child passing under.
items.notes: THE GAME (Kiss p. 206, No. 1, the same game): "Két gyermek összefogódzik, kezöket magasra fölemelik, azaz kaput alkotnak kezeikből. A többiek szintén összefogódzanak egy sorba, és átbújnak a kapun": two children join hands and raise them high, making a gate; the others join hands in a line and pass through it. At the end the gatekeepers must not let the last one through, but catch her and stand her beside the gatekeeper on the left; and so on until all are caught.
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 as the record reads it, with Kiss's 1891 spellings and our English translation, and the folk style added (the band rests); keep correcting here

dossier.function: An arch game (Újhold-játék, "new-moon game"). Two children join hands and hold them up to make a gate; the others, holding hands in a line, pass under it while everyone sings. In No. 4 the line and the gatekeepers trade the first verse: "Let us through, bridge-keeper!" "I won't let you through, bridge-keeper!", and the gate closes on the last child, who joins the gatekeepers (Kiss, pp. 206-207).
dossier.elements: F major, 2/4; a repeated four-bar call and answer (c c A A, twice, then c c c d | c A), the "Bújj, bújj" verse in eighths and quarters, and a long tail of "raj-ta, raj-ta" on F, as many as there are children to pass. Range E to d.
dossier.practice: Walking pace. The two parts of the first verse are sung by the line and by the gatekeepers in turn; the "rajta" bars are counted out, one for each child under the arch (Kiss: "a hány átbúvó van", as many as pass through).
dossier.accompaniment: None: a children's game sung while walking under the arch (Kiss's description). Band: rests. A clave on the walking beat would be our addition, and is not written.
dossier.lyrics: Hungarian. "Ereszsz által, ereszsz által, te hidasi mester!" (Let us through, let us through, you bridge-master!) / "Nem eresztlek, nem eresztlek, te hidasi mester!" (I won't let you through, I won't, you bridge-master!) / "Bújj, bújj zöldes, zöld levelestűl, nyitva van az aranykapu, csak bújjatok rajta, rajta, rajta, rajta..." (Crawl, crawl, little green one, with your green leaves; the golden gate is open, just crawl through it, through, through, through...). Kiss's spelling (ereszsz, eresztlek, levelestűl) is regional and of 1891; today's school version runs "Bújj, bújj, zöld ág, zöld levelecske, nyitva van az aranykapu, csak bújjatok rajta". Fit for class. Translation ours, to be checked.
dossier.honesty: Traditional; notes and words as Kiss printed them (Baranya county). Version 3 on the same page (Veszprém, "Bújj, bújj zöld ág, zöld leveles szál! Hányat termett a mogyoró?") is another tune for the same game, not transcribed here.
dossier.licence: Kiss Áron (1845-1908), Magyar gyermekjáték-gyűjtemény (Budapest: Hornyánszky, 1891): public domain everywhere. The MEK file is the 2000 reprint of the 1891 pages; its new preface and notes are not used.
dossier.respect: A children's game; nothing sensitive.
dossier.review: A Hungarian speaker or Kodály-trained teacher, for the words and the game.

items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): Every bar totals eight eighth units. A, bars 1-4 and 13-16, uses C major with E natural and A natural; B, bars 5-12, uses E flat and A flat. dossier.practice: Rehearsal key C/C minor; written range C4-C5. Quarter note = 100 target, start at 76. A Francophone reviewer must correct idiom and sung stress.
dossier.honesty: AI-assisted original course composition, 11 November 2026; not a Claudia Bouvette work, translation, arrangement or soundalike. The genre label identifies a listening comparison only.

items.title: Chimaycha (Ayacucho), record
items.subtitle: Women's song-dance with harp: the rhythm cell
items.source: Clip 16 of a Dust-to-Digital Instagram post (19 October 2026), via Fajardo Vilcanchos Cocas Ayacucho on Facebook; rhythm read from the recording

sourceUrls.label: Dust-to-Digital on Instagram (posted 19 October 2026), clip 16 of 20: a chimaycha performance in Ayacucho, Peru, via Fajardo Vilcanchos Cocas Ayacucho on Facebook

performances.label: chimaycha in Ayacucho: women singing in a line with harp, at night (Dust-to-Digital, October 2026, via Fajardo Vilcanchos Cocas Ayacucho)

performanceNotes: The clip is 60 seconds, filmed at night among the dancers. Chimaycha has many recordings: the Lucanamarca and Chuschi (Ayacucho) groups, the Instituto de Etnomusicología of the Pontificia Universidad Católica del Perú (Lima), and Raúl R. Romero's writings on Andean music name communities and singers.
items.blocked: Transcription: the women's high singing and the harp could not be separated by machine (the tracker jumps between them); take the melody by ear from a cleaner chimaycha recording, or from a printed collection, and the Quechua words with it. Source check: the song's name, the community (the page that posted it is named for Vilcanchos and Cocas, districts of Víctor Fajardo province; chimaycha is sung across southern Ayacucho), and whether it is an old song or a newer one by a named singer.
items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): onsets of the whole clip folded onto the cycle that repeats best (1.14 s, one 2/4 bar at about 105 beats a minute, in eight sixteenths): on each beat, strong on the first sixteenth, weak on the second, strong on the third and fourth, which is the huayno cell (an eighth and two sixteenths). The pitch tracker (F4 to C6) found F the most-sung note, then B flat, C, D flat, G and A flat.
items.kindNote: A record of the clip with its rhythm cell and the harp's bass; missing: the melody, the Quechua words, the song's name and maker, the harp's treble, and the dance steps (the women dance in a line while singing).

dossier.function: A chimaycha: a song-dance of the southern Ayacucho highlands, sung by young women in a very high, bright voice and danced in a line or circle, at night, at festivals and courting gatherings. Here a group of women in festival dress (wide hats, shawls, full skirts) sing and dance, with a harp played among them.
dossier.elements: 2/4 with the huayno cell, an eighth and two sixteenths on each beat; a minor pentatonic melody (the pitches heard most are F, A flat, B flat, C and E flat, with D flat), sung high over the harp's bass; short phrases repeated in pairs.
dossier.practice: About 105 beats a minute, steady; the harp's bass marks every beat and its treble the cell; the singers' voices are very high (up to C6) and loud.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: a harp (the Ayacucho arpa, played seated or carried), often a violin and a guitar or charango, with the women singing. Source: the clip, and the genre's usual band. In class: the band's bass on the beats and a guitar or ukulele on the cell, once the melody is known.
dossier.lyrics: Not taken: the words are Quechua and not clear in the recording; to be found with the song and checked by a Quechua speaker from Ayacucho.
dossier.honesty: Traditional genre; nothing of this song's melody is written here. The rhythm cell and the tempo are read from the recording (onsets folded onto a 2/4 bar); the pitch content is from the pitch tracker over the whole clip.
dossier.licence: The genre is traditional; the particular song may be old (anonymous) or by a named singer. The recording belongs to the performers and the Facebook page; no audio or video is kept here.
dossier.respect: A festive and courting genre, nothing sacred; credit the community and the singers. Present it as women's singing of the Ayacucho highlands, in Quechua.
dossier.review: A chimaycha singer or a Quechua speaker from Ayacucho; an ethnomusicologist of Andean song for the song's name.

items.title: De Bellringers, handbells (chord reading)
items.subtitle: Handbell team in a Dutch church: the harmony of 27 seconds
items.source: Clip 19 of a Dust-to-Digital Instagram post (19 October 2026), De Bellringers (@debellringers); chords read from the recording

sourceUrls.label: Dust-to-Digital on Instagram (posted 19 October 2026), clip 19 of 20: a handbell performance by @debellringers in the Netherlands

performances.label: De Bellringers, a handbell team, ringing in a church in the Netherlands (Dust-to-Digital, October 2026)

performanceNotes: The clip is 27 seconds: about eight ringers in a line at a padded table in front of a Gothic-revival altar, each with two or more bells. De Bellringers post their own videos on Instagram (@debellringers), where the piece may be named.
items.blocked: Source check: name the piece (ask De Bellringers); if it is a hymn or folk tune in the public domain, take its melody from a printed source and keep this harmony reading only as a check; if it is a modern composition or arrangement, keep only the record and the ringing technique. Transcription: the chords are a machine reading of 27 seconds; a ringer should check them.
items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): the bell onsets fall every 0.39-0.43 s (eighths at about 75 a minute); from 1.7 s, each 0.8 s beat was reduced to its strongest pitches (harmonic salience, room tone subtracted) and matched to major and minor triads. The second section (13.7 s on) matched clearly (scores 0.45-0.57); the first less so (0.31-0.46). Overall the clip sits in A flat major and C minor (G sharp, F and D sharp, that is A flat, F and E flat, are the strongest pitch classes).
items.kindNote: The chord sequence only, read from 27 seconds; missing: the piece's name, composer and arranger, its melody, the voicing (which bells sound in each chord), and the ringing techniques used (one ringer bends to the table to change bells).

dossier.function: Concert handbell ringing: a team rings a piece as one instrument, each ringer responsible for two to four notes (one bell in each hand, more on the table), so every chord is made by several people at once.
dossier.elements: Harmony is the point. A first section in C minor (C minor, F minor, G, C major, A flat, B flat), then a second in A flat major whose chords move in pairs of beats: A flat, E flat, D flat (or F minor), A flat, E flat, B flat, ending on C major. The bells ring on and blend, so each chord sounds as a held wash; the top line moves mostly by step.
dossier.practice: About 75 beats a minute, with a ring every eighth note in the inner parts; the bells are left to ring through each chord, so how and when they are damped shapes the changes. Quiet and resonant, in a stone church.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: handbells alone (English handbells, three to five octaves). The two voices here ring the chords; in class: chime bars or handbells shared out, each pupil one or two notes, ringing when the chord contains their note.
dossier.lyrics: None: instrumental (if the piece is a hymn, its words belong to the hymn's own record).
dossier.honesty: A reading of one team's harmony. The chords were found by matching major and minor triads to the strongest pitches in each beat; the beat grid, the bar lines and the spelling are ours. No melody is written.
dossier.licence: Unknown: the piece is not named and may be a modern composition or arrangement still in copyright, so only the chord sequence is kept. The recording belongs to De Bellringers; no audio or video is kept here.
dossier.respect: Rung in a church; the piece may be sacred. Name the team; if it is a hymn, present it as one.
dossier.review: De Bellringers themselves, for the piece and the ringing; a handbell director for the chords.

items.title: Dle Yaman
items.subtitle: Armenian folk song, for duduk and drone (dam)
items.source: Vardan Oleyan, duduk, in a clip posted by Dust-to-Digital on Instagram (October 2026); draft transcription by pitch tracking

sourceUrls.label: Dust-to-Digital on Instagram (posted October 2026): Vardan Oleyan, duduk, with a second duduk holding the dam

performances.label: Vardan Oleyan, duduk, with a second duduk on the dam (Dust-to-Digital, October 2026)

performanceNotes: The clip this draft was taken from (4 min 8 s, the tune played twice). A sung performance, and Komitas's printed setting, still to find.
items.blocked: Source check: an automatic draft from one duduk performance (pitch-tracked by machine, rhythm fitted by hand to 4/4); compare by ear with the Dust-to-Digital clip and with a printed source, ideally Komitas's own setting, before trusting any note. The Armenian words are missing. Classroom check: the class as damkash (everyone holds the low B drone, breathing in turns so it never stops) under one melody player.
items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-10): the clip's audio (4 min 8 s) was pitch-tracked with the steady drone subtracted; the drone is B (247.6 Hz, B3 at A=440, 5 cents sharp). The performance plays the tune twice (0:02-2:11 and 2:13-4:03); both passes agree on the notes, and the second, cleaner one decided the few disagreements. Each phrase takes about 12 seconds, so at 1/4=60 each phrase is three bars here.

dossier.function: A slow lyrical Armenian folk song, here played as an instrumental on two duduks: the lead carries the melody and its ornaments, the second holds the dam, a continuous drone on the keynote.
dossier.elements: Melody over a drone: one held B under everything. The tune lives in five notes above it (C sharp, D, E, F sharp, G) and only falls to the drone's B at the two cadences; three sections, the first high (around F sharp and G), the second and third low (around D and E), each phrase a short turn into a long held note.
dossier.practice: Very slow and free in the original (no steady beat; the long notes swell with vibrato); this setting fits it to 4/4 at 1/4=60 so the page can count it in, and the held notes may be stretched freely. The drone never breaks: the damkash uses circular breathing; a class can share it by breathing at different times.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: two duduks, the lead on the melody and the damkash holding the dam on the keynote; the dam is the only accompaniment. Source: the Dust-to-Digital clip and its caption. The band plays nothing here (drums, bass and chords off); the drone is the second voice, for the class to hold or the page to play.
dossier.lyrics: Missing: the song has Armenian words, but this draft is from an instrumental performance and none are written here. Words, transliteration and translation still to find, from a printed source, and to be checked by an Armenian speaker before any are sung in class.
dossier.honesty: Traditional melody. This is a draft of one 2026 performance: the pitches were taken by a pitch tracker and checked against the recording's timing, the ornaments were reduced to plain eighths, and the bar lines and note lengths are ours. Every G was played about 40 cents flat, between F sharp and G; the notation writes a plain G.
dossier.licence: The melody is a traditional Armenian folk song (public domain). The recording and video belong to the performers and Dust-to-Digital: only the melody was taken down, and no audio or video is kept here.
dossier.respect: A song of longing, and one often heard at Armenian commemorations; present it as a serious song, not a novelty instrument demo. Name the player and the duduk.
dossier.review: A duduk player or Armenian musician, for the mode, the flat G and the ornaments; ideally someone who can supply the words.

items.title: Koneka bamboo band
items.subtitle: A Bougainville school bamboo band: the call and the chord loop
items.source: Clip 15 of a Dust-to-Digital Instagram post (19 October 2026), via Dominic Kokomo; draft transcription by machine, from the recording

sourceUrls.label: Dust-to-Digital on Instagram (posted 19 October 2026), clip 15 of 20: students performing at the Koneka Primary School in Arawa, Papua New Guinea, via Dominic Kokomo

performances.label: Koneka Primary School students, Arawa, Bougainville, on bamboo pipes (Dust-to-Digital, October 2026, via Dominic Kokomo)

performanceNotes: The clip is 28 seconds, outdoors at the school. Bougainville bamboo bands are well recorded; the Institute of Papua New Guinea Studies (Port Moresby) holds field recordings, and many school and village bamboo bands post their own.
items.blocked: Source check: what piece the children play, and whether it is a traditional Bougainville tune, a church song or a local band's composition; ask the school (via Dominic Kokomo). Transcription: the opening call, the chord loop, its rhythm and its bass are read; check the voicing by ear (which pipes sound in each chord), and whether a tune runs over the loop that this recording does not let through.
items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): the clip's sustained part (harmonic/percussive separation) was pitch-tracked for the call (0.3-5.0 s: A4, then D5 D5 B4 B4 C sharp 5 C sharp 5 A4 A4, twice, each note struck twice at 0.31 s); from 5.05 s every beat (0.975 s) was reduced to its strongest pitches and matched to major and minor triads, giving the sequence D D D | G Bm A D | G Bm A D | D D | G Bm A D | G Bm A D | D D, with the low pipes on G3, B2, A2 and D3. In each beat the band strikes twice, on the beat and 0.26-0.33 s later.
items.kindNote: The whole 28-second clip as heard (a call on one pipe, then the band's chord loop); missing: the piece's name and maker, the rest of the piece, how the pipes are shared out among the players, and any dance or singing that goes with it.

dossier.function: A school bamboo band: a crowd of children, each blowing one or two long bamboo pipes, with older players on bundled panpipes; played outdoors for an audience at the school.
dossier.elements: Harmony is the point. A single pipe calls first, D, B, C sharp, A, each note struck twice; then the whole band answers with a loop of four chords in D major, G, B minor, A, D (IV, vi, V, I), one chord to each dotted-quarter beat of a 6/8, each chord struck short then long; the call's notes are the chords' top line, and the long pipes take the roots, with the D chord held for three beats at the end of each pass. The pipes are tuned close to D major but not exactly (the B flat heard against the D chord is about 10 cents flat of equal temperament and may be a pipe tuned between A and B flat).
dossier.practice: 6/8 at about 63 dotted-quarter beats a minute (eighths 0.31 s), one chord per beat, struck on the beat and again an eighth later; every pipe sounds on its beat, so the whole band moves together like a choir. Each child owns one or two notes and plays only when that note is in the chord; the pipe lengths, from the size of the children's arms up to two metres, give the bass.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: the pipes alone (Bougainville bamboo bands may also strike the ends of large pipes with rubber sandals for the bass). Here the two voices carry the chords and the bass, and the band is off; in class, the chord tones shared out like handbells: each pupil one note, played when the chord contains it.
dossier.lyrics: None: instrumental.
dossier.honesty: A reading of one school band. The call was pitch-tracked from the first five seconds (one pipe alone); the chords and bass were read by machine from the strongest pitches of each beat and checked by matching triads; the rhythm from the strokes. The voicing (call notes on top, roots below) is ours, as are the bar lines and the spelling.
dossier.licence: Unknown: the piece is not named. A chord loop as such is common property; the call and the piece as a whole may belong to a local composer. The recording belongs to the school and Dominic Kokomo; no audio or video is kept here.
dossier.respect: Children filmed at their school: name the school and keep to the music, no images. Bougainville's bamboo bands are a point of local pride; present them as a living tradition, not as a curiosity.
dossier.review: A Bougainville musician or teacher at Koneka Primary School, for the piece's name and how the pipes are shared out.

Classroom check: how far down the chain to go (it ends with Death and God; a class may stop at the blacksmith), and how the chain fits the music, which the book does not write out.
items.notes: THE CHAIN (Hague, p. 99): "Each verse adds an animal, and the whole list is repeated." Verse 2: "La Rana se sale a pasear, / Viene el Raton y se trina, / El Raton, la Rana, la Araña, la Rana, / Cantando debajo del agua." The list: La Araña, la Rana; la Rana, el Raton; el Raton, el Gato; el Gato, el Perro; el Perro, el Palo; el Palo, la Lumbre; la Lumbre, el Agua; el Agua, el Buey; el Buey, el Cochino; el Cochino, el Herrero; el Herrero, la Muerte; la Muerte, Dios. In English: the spider and the frog, the frog and the rat, the rat and the cat, the cat and the dog, the dog and the stick, the stick and the light, the light and the water, the water and the ox, the ox and the pig, the pig and the blacksmith, the blacksmith and Death, Death and God.
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with the verse's last bar as written here (a quarter and a held half for Hague's two quarters under a fermata), the chain and verse 2 as text, and the waltz style added; keep correcting here

dossier.function: A cumulative children's song: each verse brings a new creature or thing out to sing with the frog under the water, and the whole chain is sung back each time (spider, frog, rat, cat, dog, stick, fire, water, ox, pig, blacksmith, Death, God). It ends with everyone croaking "ga-ra, ga-ra", the last croak held as long as breath lasts.
dossier.elements: D major, 3/4, a range of a ninth (A below middle C to the B above it); quarters with one sixteenth pickup and one pair of eighths; the croaking coda in 2/4 on one note.
dossier.practice: The verse sung by everyone; the chain added verse by verse (a memory game); the "ga-ra" croaks ad lib, the last one held a long time (Hague's note).
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the notes, Spanish words and English singing translation as Hague printed them from Mrs. Dane Coolidge's singing. The fermata bar is lengthened to fill the metre (see the N: lines).
dossier.licence: Eleanor Hague (1875-1954), Spanish-American Folk-Songs, Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society 10 (1917): public domain in the US (published 1917) and in Canada (Hague d. 1954).
dossier.respect: A children's song; the chain ends "La Muerte, Dios" (Death, God), which a teacher may choose to sing or leave.
dossier.review: A Spanish-speaking teacher, for the words and the chain.
dossier.accompaniment: The record transcribes the voice alone; no traditional accompaniment is documented here. Band: the waltz style, a plain 3/4 accompaniment for a children's song (conservative guess, 11 November 2026)
dossier.lyrics: Spanish with Hague's English singing translation under the notes; verse 2 and the whole chain (p. 99) as text. All fit for class; the chain ends with Death and God (la Muerte, Dios), and a class may stop at the blacksmith (conservative guess, 11 November 2026)

items.title: Mafuve
items.subtitle: Dance of girls: Ndau dance song with four clap parts
items.source: Natalie Curtis Burlin, Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (New York: G. Schirmer, 1920), "Mafuve: Dance of Girls", pp. 103-105 (words and dance pp. 29-30)

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Curtis, Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (1920), p. 103 (music with the four clap parts; continues pp. 104-105)
the same, pp. 29-30: the dance, and the words with Curtis's translation

performanceNotes: No recording of this song found. Curtis made phonograph records of the singers (book, p. xxv), not yet located (Columbia University, the Library of Congress and the Smithsonian are the likely places). For the style of Ndau singing with clapping, the International Library of African Music (ILAM, Rhodes University) holds many Ndau recordings: digitalarchives.ru.ac.za, search "Ndau"; listen and choose one before linking.
items.blocked: Source check against pp. 103-105 (the whole song is now transcribed, 2026-11-11): especially the low grunted bars marked * ("O ha o", E-G sharp-B below the staff), the sextuplet and quintuplet figures, and the two closing bars, where the 32nd-note groups are read approximately. Then (the sextuplet clap figures, and "e" at the end of bar 4 against "e yo-we" at the start of bar 5), a Chindau speaker for the words, and a classroom try: four groups, one clap part each, two dancers stamping in the middle.
items.notes: THE CLAPS (p. 103), one bar each, in sixteenths of a 3/4 bar: 1. two eighths (accented) | an eighth-note triplet, the last tied over | a sextuplet: (tie), clap, (hold), clap, (hold), rest. 2. (the dancers only) rest, clap, rest, clap | rest | rest. 3. four sixteenths | a sextuplet: eighth, eighth, sixteenth, sixteenth | two eighths. 4. eighth and two sixteenths | sixteenth, eighth, two thirty-seconds | three sixteenths and a rest. A footnote gives a quintuplet as another rhythm for beats 2 and 3 of the third part.
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with the six-in-a-beat groups of bars 12, 13, 26 and 30, the five-in-a-beat group of bar 22 and the thirty-seconds of bars 31-32 as read here (bars counted from the first full bar; this record's UNCERTAIN line calls bar 22 "bar 18"), the underlay of bars 26 and 30 corrected to p. 105 (bar 26: "i we i ye i ye _ e we yo we"; bar 30: "e ya e ya e ya _ e we yo we"; this record's w: lines still need the same fix), Curtis's English for bars 31-32 added under the closing line, %%style folk, the %%band clap parts kept, and Curtis's colonial framing kept out, with a one-sentence teacher's note on it; keep correcting here

dossier.function: A dance song of girls and young women (Ndau, central Mozambique). It tells of a young bride who, though she loves her husband and her new home, longs for her mother and her childhood home: "Alas, my mother's home! I left my mother's home; I love my husband's home." Two girls dance at a time, facing each other, starting with two stamps; the others stand round them in a circle, clapping and singing, until their turn (Curtis pp. 29-30, from C. Kamba Simango).
dossier.elements: 3/4 at quarter = 63; E major; each bar a call on the first beat ("E-yo-we", "Kwa-mai-we") then a quick falling run of vocables (F E D C C: "we yo we i-ye"); the first beat carries the words and the dancers' two stamps, the rest is "parenthetical", carried by quicker clapping (Curtis's note under the music). Range B below middle C to B.
dossier.practice: Not fast. The song is repeated and recombined at will: "any phrase or group of phrases of this song may be repeated an indefinite number of times, so the song may be sung for an hour, or an hour and a half, steadily. There is no prescribed order" (Curtis, p. 105). In class: four groups take one clap rhythm each, two dancers stamp on the first beat and do the second clap; everyone sings.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: "No drums are used, the song being accompanied by the clapping of hands" (p. 29). Curtis prints four hand-clap rhythms under the voice and explains (p. 105) that no one keeps one rhythm all through: each clapper changes every two or three bars, but "a chorus of clapping, composed of all four rhythms sounding at the same time, is always heard" once the song is under way. The second rhythm (16th rest, clap, 16th rest, clap on the first beat) belongs to the two dancers. Band here: the four rhythms exactly as printed, each on its own sound so the layers can be told apart (clap, claves, wood block, rim), and the dancers' two stamps on the kick; all of these are hand claps and feet in the tradition. No bass, no chords.
dossier.lyrics: Chindau with Curtis's singing translation. Mostly vocables (eyo'we, we yo'we iye); the words proper: "Kwa'mai-we" (my mother's home), "Kwa'mai nda lega" (I left my mother's home), "Ndo da kwumisha" (I love my husband's home). Fit for class as a song about missing home. Curtis's own aside (women marry very young) is left out. Spelling to be checked by a Chindau speaker.
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the notes, words, accents and the four clap parts as Curtis printed them from C. Kamba Simango and other Ndau singers. Only the sounds of the layers are ours (in the tradition they are all hand claps).
dossier.licence: Natalie Curtis Burlin (d. 1921), Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (G. Schirmer, 1920): public domain in the US and in Canada (Simango d. 1966, out of copyright under the life-plus-50 term then in force).
dossier.respect: A social dance song, nothing sacred. Credit C. Kamba Simango. The book's general framing ("Dark Continent", remarks on race) stays out of the record; Curtis's description of the dance and the clapping is kept.
dossier.review: A Chindau speaker, for the words; a teacher of southern African dance, for the stamps and the circle.

items.title: Mu-to-to-li'le
items.subtitle: Drip-drop the rain: Ndau children's song
items.source: Natalie Curtis Burlin, Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (New York: G. Schirmer, 1920), Children's Songs I, p. 106 (game notes p. 30)

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent, at p. 106

items.blocked: Source check: compare with Curtis p. 106 (Children's Songs I), especially the sixteenths against the eighths (all of bars 2-4 are sixteenths but the last note) and the stress ticks. Ask someone who speaks Chindau to hear the words and the stresses before it is published.
items.notes: THE GAME (Curtis, p. 30): "This song is sung by children when playing in the rain. They call the raindrops to pour down till all the pools are full." They swim in the pools and spear the big red-breasted bullfrogs with little pointed sticks. "To-to" is the sound of rain falling in drops.
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with nothing guessed, %%style folk, the band silent as before, and Curtis's colonial framing kept out, with a one-sentence teacher's note on it; keep correcting here

dossier.function: A rain game: children sing it while playing in the rain, calling the drops to fall until the pools are full, so they can swim, and hunt the big red-breasted bullfrogs. "To-to" is the sound of rain falling in drops (Curtis's note, from Simango).
dossier.elements: Four bars of 3/4 in quick sixteenths on four notes (E G A B), every bar opening "To-to li-le" with both syllables of "To-to" stressed: the stress falls on the pickup and on the downbeat, against the bar.
dossier.practice: Not fast (quarter = 60, Curtis). Sung by children, unaccompanied; the band rests. The stress ticks are part of the song: Curtis prints them over every "To" and "to".
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the notes, words and stress marks as Curtis printed them from C. Kamba Simango's singing. The English line is Curtis's singing translation, fitted to the same notes.
dossier.licence: Natalie Curtis Burlin (d. 1921), Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (G. Schirmer, 1920): public domain in the US (published 1920) and in Canada (Curtis d. 1921; Simango, who gave the songs, d. 1966, so also out of copyright under the life-plus-50 term then in force).
dossier.respect: A children's game song, nothing sacred. Credit C. Kamba Simango, who brought the Ndau songs to the book. Take the notes and Curtis's game notes, not the book's general commentary, which has dated generalisations about race.
dossier.review: A Chindau speaker, for the words and the stresses.
dossier.accompaniment: none: children sing it while playing in the rain and the plate has the voice alone; the band rests (conservative guess, 11 November 2026)
dossier.lyrics: Chindau with Curtis's singing English, all sung, nothing left out; meaning from Curtis's appendix: to-to, the sound of rain falling in drops; lile, pour down; rain, let it rain (the appendix spells it "mfula ngaine", the plate "mv'langa ine"); makandwa azale, the pools full; tizo bumwila, we shall swim; macheche, the red-breasted bullfrog; spelling and stresses for a Chindau speaker (conservative guess, 11 November 2026)

items.title: Muvi'li, zu'ma, zu'ma
items.subtitle: Drying chant: Ndau children's game
items.source: Natalie Curtis Burlin, Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (New York: G. Schirmer, 1920), Children's Songs III, p. 106 (game notes p. 31)

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent, at p. 106

items.blocked: Source check: compare with Curtis p. 106 (Children's Songs III). Classroom check: jump on each beat while chanting; does the one-line rhythm read well in the rhythm views, and should it live there rather than with the tunes?
items.notes: THE GAME (Curtis, p. 31): "After the children have been swimming, they jump up and down in the sun to shake the water off and dry themselves. They sing this little half-spoken song while jumping in time to each beat of the music." They think the song and the leaping are a kind of charm that helps make them dry.
items.decisionNote: reviewed 11 November 2026 and fit for class, but not published as a tune: it is a spoken chant written on one percussion line, which the page would play as a pitched B. It belongs in the rhythm views (course/rhythms) as a chant with its stamps; kept here until it is written that way.

dossier.function: A drying chant: after swimming the children jump up and down in the sun to shake the water off, chanting this and jumping on each beat; they hold the chant and the leaping to be a charm that dries them (Curtis, p. 31, from Simango).
dossier.elements: Rhythm only, spoken: twelve bars of 2/4 in eighths and quarters, the refrain "Mu-vi-li, zu-ma, zu-ma!" four times with "Ka-si-la" and "O-mai" between, each of those stressed on its first syllable.
dossier.practice: Rather quickly (quarter = 116, Curtis). Half spoken; one jump on each beat. The band plays only a soft low thump on the beat for the jumps; the notes are on one line because the chant has no pitch.
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the rhythm and words as Curtis printed them from C. Kamba Simango; the English line is Curtis's ("Bo-dy, bo-dy, dry off quick!"). The thump on the beat is ours.
dossier.licence: Natalie Curtis Burlin (d. 1921), Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (G. Schirmer, 1920): public domain in the US and in Canada (Simango d. 1966, out of copyright under the life-plus-50 term then in force).
dossier.respect: A children's game, nothing sacred. Credit C. Kamba Simango. Leave out Curtis's remark beneath the plate comparing African and African-American accentuation; keep her game notes.
dossier.review: A Chindau speaker, for the words and stresses.
dossier.accompaniment: none but the children's jumping; the band plays only a soft low thump on each beat for the jumps (ours) (conservative guess, 11 November 2026)
dossier.lyrics: Chindau, spoken, with Curtis's English, all chanted, nothing left out; meaning from Curtis's appendix: muvili (mufili), body; zuma, dry off; kasila, quick; o-mai, dry ("you are dry" understood); spelling and stresses for a Chindau speaker (conservative guess, 11 November 2026)

items.title: Na Bahia tem
items.subtitle: In Bahia there is: Brazilian sung dance in two lines
items.source: Alexina de Magalhães Pinto, Cantigas das creanças e do povo e danças populares (Rio de Janeiro: F. Alves, 1916), p. 15; the dance pp. 109-112

sourceUrls.label: Senado Federal digital library: Alexina de Magalhães Pinto, Cantigas das creanças e do povo e danças populares (1916), the original edition; the song at p. 15, the dance pp. 109-112

performances.label: children's roda version on YouTube (title checked, not yet listened to)

performanceNotes: The Senado Federal's 2023 re-edition of the same book (handle id/11111) includes a recording of this melody, 02_Na_Bahia.wav; its licence is not stated, so it is listed here, not linked. No archival recording by tradition-bearers found yet; the Museu do Folclore Edison Carneiro (Rio) and the Instituto Moreira Salles collections are the places to ask.
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Alexina p. 15 (the two sixteenths on "Seu bem", and the key signature: two sharps on the first staff, one on the second; the tune has no C, so they agree) and the dance version pp. 109-110, where small crosses mark the claps (the scan is faint there: the claps here follow her written description on p. 112). The dance version's polka ("Dansam polka", p. 110: eight bars of 2/4 in E flat for piano alone, two four-bar phrases each ending on a chord) was tried on 2026-11-11 and not transcribed: in this scan its right-hand thirds and sixths blur together, so the top line cannot be read reliably. It wants a sharper copy of the 1916 edition (Biblioteca Nacional, Rio, or another library's scan); until then the band's march-and-polka style stands in for it, as the accompaniment note says. The sung dance itself (pp. 109-110) is the same tune as p. 15, in E flat and 4/4 with the claps marked. A Portuguese speaker for the words; classroom check: the two facing lines, three steps and three claps forward, three back.
items.notes: THE DANCE (p. 112): "dispõem-se em duas fileiras, cada cavalheiro em frente á sua dama ... dão tres passos para a frente, batendo palmas tres vezes, uma em cada passo; (as palmas vão assignaladas na musica por uma cruzinha +) ... dão tres passos para traz." Then en avant and back again, a greeting, the traversez, and from bar 16 a polka in pairs.
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 as the song of p. 15 with its claps, without the dance version's polka (too blurred in this scan to read), the sixteenths on "Seu bem" marked as a guess, and the march style added as the record's own stand-in; keep correcting here

dossier.function: A sung dance of two facing lines (dança cantada, em fileiras, ao som de palmas), from Rio, Bahia and Minas Gerais; in Minas, children danced it. The words name what "Bahia has": a penny coconut, a glass lamp, a flat-iron, a sewing machine; Bahia was the colony's first seat, where novelties came in (Alexina's note, after Sílvio Romero).
dossier.elements: 2/4, eight bars in two lines with a repeat; D major (the tune uses D E F# G A B, no C); a range of a sixth, D to B; eighths and quarters with one pair of sixteenths; the "tem, tem, tem" falls step by step (A G F# E), the second line answers it and ends on D.
dossier.practice: The dance (Alexina p. 112): two lines, each boy facing his partner about seven steps away. Bars 1-2, three steps forward, clapping on each step; bars 3-4, three steps back, singing and clapping; bars 5-6 forward again, 7-8 back. Then they greet each other and may cross over (traversez), the lines changing places; bars 9-16 forward and back again; from bar 16 everyone dances a polka in pairs to the end. One line can sing the first two lines and the other answer, all joining for the rest, and the forward-and-back can be replaced by other quadrille figures.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: hand claps by the dancers, marked with small crosses in Alexina's score (p. 109), three per two bars, one on each step; in the dance version a polka follows, which she gives with piano. The wider Bahian practice (samba de roda) adds the viola machete, pandeiro and scraped plate (prato e faca), per the UNESCO inscription of samba de roda; that is a different, adult setting and is not used here. Band here: claps only, three in every two bars on the steps (beats 1 and 2 of the first bar, beat 1 of the second). No bass, no chords; for the polka part, the band's march-and-polka style would be the stand-in. Needs nothing new for this part.
dossier.lyrics: Portuguese (1916 spelling: engommar, creanças). The score underlays "Na Bahia tem, tem, tem, tem, Na Bahia tem, seu bem, côco de vintém": "In Bahia there is, there is, there is, in Bahia there is, my dear, a penny coconut." Other verses (p. 111): "Na Bahia tem, vou mandar buscar lampeão de vidro, ó bahiana, ferro de engommar" (I'll send for a glass lamp, Bahian girl, and a flat-iron); "... machina de costura, seu bem, folle de soprar" (a sewing machine, my dear, a bellows). All fit for class. Alexina notes the verses are endless and that the ones sent with the dance were boasting challenge verses, which she leaves out; so do we.
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the tune, words and dance as Alexina de Magalhães Pinto printed them in 1916 (the tune "Rio, Bahia, Minas"; the dance as sent from Minas by Dr. G. Eutropio). The clap placement follows her description.
dossier.licence: Alexina de Magalhães Pinto (1870-1921), Cantigas das creanças e do povo e danças populares (Rio de Janeiro: Francisco Alves, 1916), Bibliotheca infantil: public domain in the US (1916), Canada and Brazil (d. 1921). The scan is published by the Senado Federal library under a Creative Commons licence; the notes here are read from it, not copied from the 2023 re-edition.
dossier.respect: The same words are sung in Umbanda as a ponto for the Baianos and the Erês (child spirits); this record is the children's dance from 1916, and a teacher may say so if asked. The book has a section of "cantigas dos pretos" whose dialect may caricature; nothing from it is used here.
dossier.review: A Portuguese speaker (Brazilian), for the words and the 1916 spellings; a Brazilian teacher who knows the roda, for the dance.

items.title: Cumbia Switch
items.subtitle: Original Grade 1 call-and-response song for voices and percussion
items.source: Grand Central Stationery, "Cumbia Switch" (original course composition, 11 November 2026), canonical source in this private workshop record, CC0 1.0

sourceUrls.label: CC0 1.0 public-domain dedication applied to this original course composition

performanceNotes: No source performance exists. The first recording should be a classroom demo made with participant consent, with real scraper, hand-drum or clap answers in bars 4 and 6; the Band's playback leaves those bars to the class.
items.blocked: The original is fully notated with words on every sung note, and the listening link is Sony Music Colombia's official upload of the CBS recording, but it has not been tried with students. A Grade 1 classroom teacher must trial the leader/class/percussion turn-taking and the two silent answer bars at 88-104; a Colombian music educator must review the history and context language, decide whether "Cumbia" may stay in the title, and say which Bermúdez recording best serves the lesson (sources disagree on when the song was first recorded); a second score reader must check the notes, words and cues.
items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): No source plate exists because this is a new composition. Bar-by-bar audit: bar 1 call G-G-A-G (four eighths); bar 2 sung answer E-E-G (two eighths and a quarter); bar 3 call G-G-A-A (four eighths), ending open on la; bar 4 two quarter rests, the first percussion answer; bar 5 call A-G-A-G (four eighths); bar 6 two quarter rests, the second percussion answer; bar 7 everyone E-G-A-G (four eighths); bar 8 E4 quarter and a quarter rest, the close on mi. Every bar totals two quarter beats; the only pitches are E4, G4 and A4; range E4-A4; the largest leap is the minor third between E and G; durations are eighths, quarters and quarter rests only. The calls rise toward la and the answers settle on mi, the resting tone of a mi-so-la song. Originality: the eighth-note so-so-la-so call is a common mi-so-la playground shape; the tune was checked against "Colombia Tierra Querida", "Rain, Rain, Go Away", "Lucy Locket" and "Bounce High, Bounce Low" and shares no phrase with them.

dossier.function: original Grade 1 call-and-response game song in which a leader's sung call is answered first by the class's voices and then by two percussion groups
dossier.elements: eight bars in 2/4 with no pickup; pitch set mi-so-la only (E4, G4, A4), written range E4-A4; paired eighth notes, quarter notes and quarter rests only; bar 1 leader's call, bar 2 class's sung answer, bar 3 leader's call, bar 4 silent bar for percussion group 1, bar 5 leader's call, bar 6 silent bar for percussion group 2, bars 7-8 everyone together, ending on mi with a quarter rest; largest leap a minor third
dossier.practice: Quarter note = 104 is the target; begin at 88 with a steady pat on both beats of every bar. The written range E4-A4 lies inside the young-unison C4-D5 range, and C major (mi-so-la on E-G-A) is the rehearsal key. Teach in steps: everyone pats the two-beat pulse; teacher sings each call and the class echoes; then the class answers bar 2 with its own words; then hand out scrapers, hand drums or claps and let the two groups answer bars 4 and 6 with the rhythm and colour the cues choose; finish with everyone singing and playing bars 7-8
dossier.accompaniment: %%style march is the Band's generic two-beat march-and-polka groove, chosen for an unmistakable strong-weak 2/4 pulse; it is not cumbia, porro or any Colombian style and must not be called one. No chord symbols are written; the Band harmonises the three notes itself. The silent bars 4 and 6 belong to classroom percussion: a scraper (any classroom guiro or washboard), a hand drum and claps
dossier.lyrics: Original English words written for this record, one syllable per sung note: "Who will an-swer?" (leader) "We will sing!" (class) "Who will play it?" (leader, then percussion) "Now an-oth-er!" (leader, then percussion) "All to-geth-er, play!" (everyone). Stressed syllables fall on the beats (WHO will AN-swer; NOW an-OTH-er). No Spanish words are used, so the song does not borrow the reference's language
dossier.honesty: AI-assisted original composition for Grand Central Stationery, 11 November 2026, under human-directed grade, range and teaching constraints. It is not traditional, not collected from a community and not modelled on "Colombia Tierra Querida" or any cumbia melody; the recording is a listening bridge only
dossier.licence: CC0 1.0. Grand Central Stationery dedicates the melody, words and this ABC encoding to the public domain to the extent legally possible. Lucho Bermúdez's composition and the CBS/Sony recording remain the copyright of their owners and are not included; the class listens through the linked official upload
dossier.respect: Name Lucho Bermúdez, Colombia and its Caribbean coast, and teach cumbia's Indigenous, African and Spanish roots and its many regional lineages. Do not claim that this classroom tune, its march groove or its percussion answers are cumbia, and do not hand out "Colombian" costumes or caricatures. Whether "Cumbia" may stay in the title is for the Colombian reviewer to decide
dossier.review: Grade 1 classroom music teacher, Colombian music educator, second score reader; all reviews still required

composition.elements: duration (2/4; quarter notes, paired eighths and quarter rests, with two whole bars of rest for an instrumental answer), timbre (voice answered by scraper, hand drum or claps), form (call and response: the leader calls, the class or a percussion group answers), pitch (mi-so-la only)
composition.listen: Lucho Bermúdez y Su Orquesta — "Colombia Tierra Querida" (CBS recording, ℗ 1972 CBS, Inc.), reissued on La Cumbia Colombiana (Sony Music Entertainment Colombia, 2025)
composition.bridge: Listen for a clear two-beat dance pulse, contrasting instrumental colours and a melody that invites a group response.
composition.context: Lucho Bermúdez (1912-1994), clarinettist, composer and bandleader from El Carmen de Bolívar, brought the porro and cumbia of Colombia's Caribbean coast into big dance-orchestra arrangements that were danced across Colombia and abroad; "Colombia Tierra Querida" became one of the country's best-loved songs. Cumbia grew from Indigenous, African and Spanish lineages on that coast (drums, gaitas, maracas, the scraper called guacharaca). This is a new 2/4 classroom tune, not an arrangement and not a cumbia rhythm.
composition.distance: Original notes, rhythm and words; no melody, lyric, horn line or arrangement from the recording is copied, and the classroom percussion answers are free choices, not cumbia patterns.

items.title: Sing It Up, Sing It Down
items.subtitle: Original Grade 1 contour song (draft title "Sodade Shape")
items.source: Grand Central Stationery, "Sing It Up, Sing It Down" (original course composition, 11 November 2026), canonical source in this private workshop record, CC0 1.0

sourceUrls.label: CC0 1.0 public-domain dedication applied to this original course composition

performanceNotes: No source performance exists. The first recording should be a classroom demo made with participant consent; a generated playback cannot show whether young voices keep the phrase gentle and connected.
items.blocked: The original is fully notated with words on every note, and the listening link is Lusafrica's official upload of the 1992 recording, but it has not been tried with students. A Grade 1 classroom teacher must trial the slow tempo, the breath after every second bar and the detached and accented notes; a Cabo Verdean music educator must review the morna, Kriolu and migration context and confirm the retitling away from "Sodade"; a second score reader must check the notes, words and cues.
items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): No source plate exists because this is a new composition. Legong is one of Bali's classical dances, accompanied by a gamelan in which fast interlocking parts move inside a slow cycle marked by gongs. dossier.elements: eight bars in 4/4 with no pickup; pitch set C-D-E-G-A-C (do-re-mi-so-la-high do), written range C4-C5; half notes and quarter notes only; A (bars 1-4) climbs from do to high do in the rhythm half-quarter-quarter, quarter-quarter-half; B (bars 5-8) is the exact retrograde of A, every pitch and duration in reverse order, so it falls from high do back to do in the same rhythm; the mirror line falls between bars 4 and 5, where high do is sung twice; largest leap a perfect fourth (G4-C5, at bars 4 and 5)

Answers (bars 2, 4, 10): A4-G4-A4 or E4-G4-A4 quarters and a quarter rest; bar 12 closes A4-G4 quarters and an A4 half. Pitch set A-C-D-E-G, range D4-D5, largest leap a fourth (E4 to A4, G4 to C5), no syncopation, dots or ties; every sixteenth group fills one whole beat. Form ABA (calls, quiet middle, calls).
