dossier.elements: twelve bars in 4/4 in ABA form. A (bars 1-4): two-bar call-and-answer pairs, each call A4-C5 quarters, a D5-D5-C5-A4 sixteenth group and a quarter, each answer three quarters and a quarter rest. B (bars 5-8): everyone, p, quarters and half notes, E4-G4-A4 | G4-E4-D4 | E4-G4-A4-C5 | D5-C5-A4. A (bars 9-12): the calls return and the last answer closes on A4. Teach in steps: the teacher leads the calls and the class learns the answers by ear, then the middle section, then a student leader takes the calls; hold every rest so the next call is heard
dossier.accompaniment: The page's folk style (a plain guitar-and-bass boom-chick) is chosen as a neutral school accompaniment; it is deliberately not the page's drone (tanpura and tabla) style and must not be replaced by harmonium, tabla or dholak patterns that would present the piece as qawwali. Quiet now, hear it grow: every answer comes around. Who will sing along with me? We will sing! Who will close the circle now? All of us!" "Allah Ho" is a repetition of God's name: play it for listening only, never as a sound to imitate, chant along with or use as classroom vocal material, and never sing its words in this piece. items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): No source plate exists because this is a new composition; this is the compositional audit. Every bar totals eight eighths with no pickup. Bars 5-8 repeat bars 1-4 with E flat for E and A flat for A, and bar 8 ends G4-D4 quarters and a C4 half. dossier.elements: sixteen bars in 4/4; C major, pitch set C-D-E-F-G-A-B (F only in bar 7), range C4-E5; verse (bars 1-8): bars 1, 2, 5 and 6 begin each beat with an eighth rest and enter on the offbeat with staccato notes, bars 3 and 7 answer on the beat with a dotted quarter and eighth (tam-ti), bars 4 and 8 hold a half note then rest two beats; chorus (bars 9-16): bars 9-12 are four one-bar calls and answers in the rhythm dotted quarter, three eighths, quarter, group 1 sings bars 9 and 11 and group 2 answers in bars 10 and 12 (the groups are named here, not in the score); bars 13-16 all together, staccato quarters on the beat in bar 13, a half note in bar 14, tam-ti in bar 15, ending on C5; C-G (I-V) only; verse-chorus form, 8+8 bars

Teach in steps: clap beats while saying the offbeat words; sing the verse; learn both halves of the chorus as one group; split into groups 1 and 2; add a horn or recorder pair answering in the rests of bars 4 and 8.
dossier.accompaniment: Newly authored C-G (I-V) chords played by the page's pop band, chosen as a neutral, straight-eighth groove; it is not a ska rhythm section and must not be labelled ska, mento or reggae. dossier.lyrics: Original English words written for this record; every note has one syllable, and the offbeat words are short so they can be sung crisply. items.subtitle: Original 6/4 piece for two crossing layers

items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): No source plate exists because this is a new composition; the draft's opening pickup and the one-eighth "pickup" bar in the middle were removed by rewriting. Bar-by-bar audit, every bar six quarters: melody bar 1 B d B quarters, A half, G quarter; bar 2 E G C5 quarters, G half, E quarter; bar 3 F# A D5 quarters, C5 half, A quarter; bar 4 B half, A quarter, G dotted half; bars 5-8 three half notes each (E5 C5 G; D5 B G; C5 E G; A F# D); bar 9 = bar 1, bar 10 = bar 2; bar 11 F# A D5 quarters, A half, F# quarter; bar 12 = bar 4. Ostinato: three half notes (root, fifth, root) in bars 1-4 and 9-12, two dotted halves (root, fifth) in bars 5-8, ending on G3 dotted halves. Melody pitch set D-E-F#-G-A-B-C-D-E, range D4-E5, largest leaps the major sixths at the section joins (G4 up to E5 into bar 5, D4 up to B4 into bar 9) and the minor sixth C5-E4 inside bar 7, with thirds, fourths and fifths elsewhere; ostinato G3-A4. The analyzer reads the half notes that cross the 3+3 grouping as syncopation; that is the intended hemiola, not a syn-co-pa figure. Form ABA'. dossier.function: original instrumental layering piece for Grade 6: a melody group and an ostinato group play in different groupings of the same six beats, swap groupings in the middle, and a clapping group and a soloist make choices over them
dossier.elements: twelve bars in 6/4 (six quarter notes); G major, melody pitch set D-E-F#-G-A-B-C-D-E, range D4-E5; ostinato G3-A4 on chord roots and fifths; A (bars 1-4) melody in 3+3 (three quarters then a half and a quarter, or a half, quarter and dotted half) over an ostinato in three half notes; B (bars 5-8) melody in three half notes over an ostinato in two dotted halves, so the crossing swaps; A' (bars 9-12) returns with a new turn in bar 11 and the cadence on a dotted-half G; harmony G-C-D-G, C-G-C-D, G-C-D-G (I-IV-V); ABA' form
dossier.practice: Quarter note = 132 is the target; begin at 100. Rehearsal key G major; the melody's written range D4-E5 suits soprano recorder, xylophone or glockenspiel (and lies inside the young-unison C4-D5 range except two E5s, for voices on "loo"); the ostinato G3-A4 suits bass xylophone, low bells, cello or keyboard. Teach in steps: count six quarters and clap 1 and 4 (3+3), then 1, 3 and 5 (2+2+2); half the class claps each at once; learn the melody of A and B; learn the ostinato; put the layers together; swap groups; add the clapping choice in B and the soloist's interval on the last chord.
dossier.accompaniment: The ostinato (second voice) and the G-C-D chords are newly authored. The page's folk band was chosen as a plain, non-specific accompaniment; it is not chimurenga, not mbira and must not be labelled Zimbabwean. The class's two layers carry the crossing; mute the band's drums if they blur the 2+2+2 against 3+3. Do not imitate a guitar or mbira part from the recording.
dossier.lyrics: Instrumental piece for recorders, barred percussion, keyboard and body percussion; no words, so that the lesson stays on the two groupings rather than on invented text in place of Mapfumo's Shona lyrics. Any words added later should be recorded as a new adaptation.

items.title: Five Windows

dossier.function: original sung listening-bridge song for Grade 6, a counting song that makes 3+2 audible: the class sings the melody, a small group plays the ostinato, a body-percussion group chooses a grouping, and a soloist answers with a named interval in the rests
dossier.elements: twelve bars in 5/4, every bar grouped 3+2; A minor with G sharp as leading note, pitch set D-E-F-G#-A-B-C-D-E; melody D4-E5, ostinato A3-B4; A (bars 1-4): quarter, two eighths, quarter, then a half note or a half rest (bars 1, 2, 4), and five counted quarters in bar 3, with an eighth-note anacrusis "and" at the end of bar 2; B (bars 5-8): eighth-note triplets on beats 1 and 4 of bar 5 and beat 1 of bars 6 and 7, half notes on beats 4-5, the harmony moving Dm to E at the 3+2 split of bar 7, a half rest in bar 8; A' (bars 9-12) repeats A with a new cadence; Am-Dm-E (i-iv-V) only; ABA' form; intervals named in the lesson: E-A and B-E perfect fourths, C-E, F-A and E-G# major thirds, and the ostinato's A-E, D-A and E-B perfect fifths

items.title: Nine-Spoke Carousel
items.subtitle: Original 9/8 piece grouped two ways
items.source: Grand Central Stationery, "Nine-Spoke Carousel" (original course composition, 11 November 2026), canonical source in this private workshop record, CC0 1.0

performanceNotes: No source performance exists. The first recording should be a classroom demo made with participant consent; the Zakir Hussain recording is a listening reference only and is not a performance of this piece.

items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): No source plate exists because this is a new composition. Bar-by-bar audit, every bar nine eighths: A, bar 1 quarter-eighth, quarter-eighth, dotted quarter (D F# A B D5); bar 2 the same rhythm (D5 B G B A, G then A chord); bar 3 the same rhythm (F# A D5 E5 D5); bar 4 the same rhythm (C#5 B A E D, A then D chord). B, bars 5-8 three quarters and a dotted quarter each (G B D5 B; A F# D F#; B D5 B C#5; C#5 A E A). A', bars 9-10 repeat bars 1-2, bar 11 C#5 B A F# E in the A-section rhythm, bar 12 D4 held for the whole bar. Ostinato: three dotted quarters (root, fifth, fifth, or the next chord's root) in the A sections, and quarter, quarter, quarter, dotted quarter in B, ending on a full-bar D4. dossier.function: original instrumental grouping piece for Grade 6: a melody group and an ostinato group show the same nine eighths grouped 3+3+3 and then 2+2+2+3, while a clapping group chooses a grouping and a conductor changes the density on the return
dossier.elements: twelve bars in 9/8 (nine eighths); D major, melody pitch set D-E-F#-G-A-B-C#-D-E, range D4-E5; ostinato G3-E4 on chord roots and fifths; A (bars 1-4) in three dotted-quarter groups, the melody moving quarter-eighth, quarter-eighth, dotted quarter; B (bars 5-8) in 2+2+2+3, three quarters and a dotted quarter in every bar, with the ostinato in the same grouping; A' (bars 9-12) returns and closes on D4 held for the full bar of nine eighths; harmony D, G-A, D, A-D | G, D, G-A, A | D, G-A, A, D (I-IV-V); ABA' form
dossier.practice: Dotted quarter = 80 (eighth = 240) is the target; begin at eighth = 180 and count eighths aloud, "1 2 3 1 2 3 1 2 3" for A and "1 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 3" for B. items.title: Blue Engine
items.subtitle: Original 12-bar teaching blues with answer windows
items.source: Grand Central Stationery, "Blue Engine" (original course composition, 11 November 2026), canonical source in this private workshop record, CC0 1.0

sourceUrls.label: CC0 1.0 public-domain dedication applied to this original course composition

performanceNotes: No source performance exists. The first recording should be a classroom demo made with participant consent; a generated playback is not evidence that the answer windows work with students.
items.blocked: The original is fully notated and its listening reference is verified, but it has not been played by a class. A blues educator must review the history, the form and the framing of call-and-response soloing; a Grade 7 music teacher must trial the answer windows at the starting tempo; a second score reader must check the bar-by-bar audit.
items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): No source plate exists because this is a new composition. Bar-by-bar audit: bar 1 (C7) marcato G4 quarter, then G-Bb-G-C5-Bb-G-Eb eighths falling through the blues scale; bar 2 (C7) F-F#-G4, the dotted half on G closing the call; bars 3-4 (C7) whole-bar rests, the first answer window; bar 5 (F7) the call rebuilt on F7, marcato C5 then Eb5-C5-A4-C5-A4-F4; bar 6 (F7) Ab-A-C5 dotted half, the same chromatic approach as bar 2; bars 7-8 (C7) rests, the second answer window; bar 9 (G7) marcato D5 then D5-B4-G4-F4-D4; bar 10 (F7) Eb-F-Ab-F-C5-A-F; bar 11 (C7) Eb-E-G-C5-Bb-G-Eb; bar 12 (C7) C4 dotted half and a quarter rest. Every bar totals eight eighths; written range C4-Eb5; largest leap a perfect fifth (F4-C5, bar 10). This replaces the batch draft, which had a B4-C4 major-seventh drop in bar 5, a B natural against F7 and a G7 chord under the final tonic. Form AAB: bars 5-6 restate the call over IV, bars 9-12 answer it. Originality check: no stop-time hits and no beat-one riff from the reference, no Dixon words, and the call is not the opening of any well-known blues head checked ("C Jam Blues", "Bags' Groove", "Tenor Madness", "Sonnymoon for Two", "Night Train"); falling blues-scale figures like bar 1 are common property of the idiom.

dossier.function: original 12-bar teaching blues for Grade 7; the class plays the written call in each line, a soloist answers in the two bars of rest that follow, and everyone plays the closing line together
dossier.elements: 12 bars in 4/4 (three four-bar lines); chords I-I-I-I | IV-IV-I-I | V-IV-I-I in C (C7, F7, G7); written range C4-Eb5; pitch set C D Eb E F F# G Ab A Bb B (the C blues scale C Eb F F# G Bb in bars 1-2, the same shape rebuilt on the F7 chord in bars 5-6, chord tones and blue notes in bars 9-12); eighth, quarter and dotted-half notes, a closing quarter rest and whole-bar rests; bars 1-2 call, bars 3-4 rest (answer), bars 5-6 call over IV, bars 7-8 rest (answer), bars 9-12 the B line that closes on C4; largest leap a perfect fifth (F4-C5, bar 10)
dossier.practice: Quarter note = 96 with swung eighths is the target; start at 72 and raise it once the class can land the dotted half in bars 2 and 6 together. The written range C4-Eb5 goes a semitone above the young-unison C4-D5 at one note only (Eb5, bar 5); C is the rehearsal key for recorder, bells and keyboard, and the page's Transpose can move it for band instruments. Teach the call by ear first (bars 1-2), then its version over F7 (bars 5-6), then the closing line; only then open the answer windows, first with the teacher answering, then volunteers choosing one cue at a time
dossier.accompaniment: The chords are the written 12-bar changes; the page's swing style supplies a jazz-swing comp and walking bass, which is a stand-in, not a Chicago blues band. A Malian/Songhai music educator must review the style framing, the cultural context and whether the title's "Sahel" implies a style the piece does not have; a Grade 8 music teacher must trial the ground and the texture changes; a second score reader must check the audit.
items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): No source plate exists because this is a new composition. Bar-by-bar audit: bars 1-2 the Guitar ground alone (D3 quarter, F3 eighth, A3 dotted quarter, G3-F3 eighths | D3 quarter, G3 eighth, B3 dotted quarter, A3-G3 eighths), Voice rests; bars 3-4 the ground again under the Voice's D5 dotted quarter, C5 eighth, A4 half | B4 quarter, C5-B4 eighths, G4 half; bar 5 Voice A4 quarter, C5-D5 eighths, E5 and D5 quarters over a whole-bar D3; bar 6 Voice rests, Guitar answers A3 quarter, C4 eighth, D4 dotted quarter, C4-A3 eighths; bar 7 Voice B4 quarter, A4-G4 eighths, F4 and E4 quarters, Guitar dyads G3+D4, F3+C4, E3+B3, D3+A3, C3+G3 in the same rhythm; bar 8 Voice D4 whole, Guitar D3+A3 whole. Every bar of both parts totals eight eighths. Voice range D4-E5, largest leap a major third (B4-G4, bar 4); Guitar range C3-D4. Vertical check: on beats 1-3 the Voice sits an octave, sixth, third or their compounds above the Guitar; on beat 4 of bars 3 and 4 the ground's passing G3 and A3 make a brief ninth (A4 over G3) and seventh (G4 over A3) under the held voice note, resolving on the next eighth. The batch draft was one unaccompanied line that claimed mono-, homo- and polyphony and dialogue without a second part. Originality check: neither line is the vocal, guitar riff or ostinato of "Ai Du" or of other Touré recordings checked ("Diaraby", "Bonde", "Savane"); a Dorian ground built on D is common property. The analyzer reads only the Voice line and places it in Grade 5 (dotted quarter and eighth, two parts); the Grade 8 concepts, the textures and the mode, live in how the two parts combine, which it does not read.

dossier.function: original voice-and-guitar texture study for Grade 8: a guitar ground, a voice line and a short dialogue that move through monophony, polyphony, call and response and homophony, so students can name each texture by ear and then choose one for a purpose; it pairs with listening to Ali Farka Touré and Ry Cooder
dossier.elements: eight bars in 4/4, D Dorian (D E F G A B C); Voice written range D4-E5, Guitar written range C3-D4 in bass clef (sounding an octave lower on guitar); ground of two bars, D3 quarter, F3 eighth, A3 dotted quarter, G3 and F3 eighths, then D3, G3, B3 dotted quarter, A3, G3, played in bars 1-4; bars 1-2 ground alone; bars 3-4 voice D5 dotted quarter, C5 eighth, A4 half, then B4 quarter, C5-B4 eighths, G4 half over the ground; bar 5 voice A4-C5-D5-E5-D5 over a held D3; bar 6 voice rests while the guitar answers A3-C4-D4-C4-A3; bar 7 voice B4-A4-G4-F4-E4 with guitar dyads G-D, F-C, E-B, D-A, C-G in the same rhythm; bar 8 voice D4 whole note over a D-A open fifth; largest voice leap a major third (B4-G4, bar 4)
dossier.practice: Quarter note = 92 is the target; start at 72. D Dorian is the rehearsal key (no key signature; the B natural is the Dorian colour). The Voice's written range D4-E5 sits a tone above the young-unison C4-D5 at one note only (E5, bar 5); the Guitar part suits guitar, bass bars, cello or keyboard left hand. Teach the ground first by ear, then sing the voice line over it on "la", then the dialogue in bars 5-6, then the closing dyads; before each section ask the class to name the texture they are about to hear. Mute the page's Band in the mixer so the written texture is the only texture

The page's folk style (boom-chick guitar on chords found from the melody) is only a fallback; mute it for the texture lesson, because any band part turns the monophonic opening into homophony. The batch draft's drone style was dropped because the page's drone is a tanpura and tabla, another tradition's sound. No guitar figure, tuning, calabash or n'goni part from the recording is imitated
dossier.lyrics: Instrumental or sung on "la": the Voice line may be sung on a neutral syllable or played on recorder, violin or flute. No words are supplied, and no Songhai, Bambara, Fula or Tamasheq words from the recording are used or imitated

composition.elements: modal tonality (D Dorian, with its raised sixth B natural in the guitar ground and the voice); the three textures written into the parts: monophonic (the guitar ground alone, bars 1-2), polyphonic (the voice's long notes against the ground's moving eighths, bars 3-4), call and response (the voice asks over a held D, the guitar answers, bars 5-6), homophonic (guitar dyads moving with the voice in the same rhythm, bars 7-8); a repeated two-bar modal ground; the guitar's dotted quarter on the "and" of beat 2 against the voice's held notes, a gentle rhythmic displacement; arranging for purpose; improvised dialogue in the cues

composition.bridge: Hear voice and guitar converse, repeated modal ground, subtle rhythmic displacement and the space between phrases.

Bars 1 and 3: A4 F4 quarters; bars 2, 4, 6 and 8: G4 G4 eighths, F4 quarter; bars 5 and 7: A4 A4 G4 G4 eighths. Pitch set F-G-A, range F4-A4, largest interval a major third (A4 down to F4). dossier.function: original JK greeting and echo song; a leader sings a two-bar greeting and the class echoes it at once, choosing loud or soft for the first echo and singing or clapping the rhythm for the second
dossier.elements: eight bars in 2/4 (L:1/8), F major, pitch set F-G-A (do-re-mi), written range F4-A4 (a major third). Bars 1-2 call "Hel-lo, how are you?" (A4 F4 quarters, G4 G4 eighths, F4 quarter); bars 3-4 the class echoes it exactly; bars 5-6 a second call "Glad to see you here to-day" (A A G G eighths, G G eighths, F quarter) that varies the opening and keeps the same ending; bars 7-8 the class echoes it. Form: call-echo, call-echo (a a b b, with b ending like a). Note values: quarters and eighths only, no rests; every phrase ends on the tonic F4. Largest interval a major third (A4-F4). Chords F and C (I and V) for the teacher or Band only
dossier.practice: Start at quarter = 76 and reach the written 88 once the echo lands on the downbeat. Teach in steps: the teacher sings the call and gestures "your turn" with an open hand on the last note; children echo; then show a loud or soft hand sign before bar 1 (big arms, small hands); then clap the rhythm of the words instead of singing. A child may become the leader once the class echoes reliably. Breathe on each final quarter note

items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): No source plate exists because this is a new composition; this is the compositional audit. Every bar totals four eighths (2/4). Bar 1 A4 A4 eighths, F#4 quarter; bar 2 rest; bar 3 F#4 E4 eighths, D4 quarter; bar 4 rest; bar 5 A4 F#4 A4 F#4 eighths; bar 6 E4 E4 eighths, D4 quarter; bar 7 rest; bar 8 D4 quarter, quarter rest. Pitch set D-E-F#-A, range D4-A4; sung intervals are steps and minor thirds, and the only larger move is the re-entry on A4 after the silent bar 4 (the pitch the song began on). The earlier draft used the same E4-G4 two-note shape, six sung notes and one unsung note as "Bamboo Breath"; this version is rebuilt around short falling eighth-note drops and silent gaps, while "Bamboo Breath" is now held tones in a continuous phrase. The analyzer reads level 2 (rests, pentatonic); its Ontario line reads Grade 5 only because it counts the two-sharp key signature, which JK children never read. Originality: so-mi and mi-re-do fragments are common property; checked against "Rain, Rain", "Bounce High, Bounce Low", "Hot Cross Buns", "Twinkle, Twinkle" and "Frère Jacques", with no shared opening. dossier.function: original JK listening song; the class sings a short falling "drop", then one child fills the silent bar with a soft bell or leaves it silent while everyone listens until the sound is gone; at the end the choice is a short wood sound or a long bell sound
dossier.elements: eight bars in 2/4 (L:1/8), D major, pitch set D-E-F#-A (do-re-mi-so), written range D4-A4 (a perfect fifth). Bar 1 "Sil-ver drop" A4 A4 eighths, F#4 quarter; bar 2 silent; bar 3 "sil-ver drop" F#4 E4 eighths, D4 quarter (the drop falls further, to the tonic); bar 4 silent; bar 5 "lis-ten, lis-ten" A4 F#4 A4 F#4 eighths; bar 6 "far a-way" E4 E4 eighths, D4 quarter; bar 7 silent; bar 8 "Gone." D4 quarter and a quarter rest. Form: drop + gap, lower drop + gap, a two-bar answer cadencing on the tonic, a last gap and a one-word coda. Note values: eighths, quarters, quarter rests and three whole-bar (two-beat) rests; within phrases the largest interval is a minor third, and the voice re-enters on A4 after the silent bar 4 (a fifth above the last sung D4)

Teach in steps: strike one bell and ask the class to raise a hand while they still hear it; sing "Silver drop" and hold still for the gap; then let one child strike a bell softly in the gap (wrist only, "touch it like a bubble") or choose silence; finally compare a wood block's short sound with a bell's long one in bar 7. Use soft mallets and hand-held bells, never hard striking

The ballad style is chosen only because it is the quietest sustained setting; for the first lessons mute the Band so bars 2, 4 and 7 are truly silent. dossier.function: original SK breath-and-silence song for partners; one partner sings the rising call to a long tone, everyone breathes in the silent bar, and the other partner answers with the longer phrase that comes home, choosing words or a hum

Bars 1-2 "Bam-boo, bam-boo" D4 E4, G4 E4 in quarters (rising); bar 3 "breathe" A4 half note (the peak, a fourth above E4); bar 4 a silent bar for the breath; bars 5-8 one four-bar phrase "Soft wind go-ing slow-ly home": A4 G4, E4 D4 falling to the bottom, then E4 G4 rising and G4 held as a half note on the tonic. dossier.practice: The written tempo is quarter = 72 (about 6.7 seconds for the four-bar answer); begin at 80 so the answer fits one breath, and never go below 66. dossier.accompaniment: Newly authored, not traditional. No chords are written; the drone style holds a quiet tonic drone under the long tones to help children find G. composition.context: Riley Lee, an American-born shakuhachi player based in Australia, became in 1980 the first non-Japanese player to receive the rank of dai shihan (grand master). Pitch set D-E-F#-A (no fa, so the climb is pentatonic), range D4-A4, largest interval a major third. The earlier draft's cues at bars 1-2 and 5-6 fell on sung bars; now each cue covers a sung line and the silent bar after it, where a child really plays. dossier.function: original SK parade song about direction; the class marches and sings a line that climbs, one child plays a short up or down bell pattern in the gap, the class sings the line that falls, and a partner answers the first child's bells by copying or going the other way
dossier.elements: eight bars in 2/4 (L:1/8), D major pentatonic, pitch set D-E-F#-A (do-re-mi-so), written range D4-A4 (a perfect fifth). Bar 1 "Pan pa-rade goes" climbs D4 E4 F#4 A4 in eighths; bar 2 "up" A4 quarter, quarter rest; bar 3 a silent bar for the bells; bar 4 "Pan pa-rade comes" falls A4 F#4 E4 E4; bar 5 "down" D4 quarter, quarter rest; bar 6 a silent bar for the answering bells; bar 7 "ev-ry-bo-dy" F#4 F#4 E4 E4; bar 8 "home!" D4 quarter, quarter rest. Form: a rising line and a falling line, each followed by a three-beat gap for a bell answer, and a two-bar cadence on the tonic. Note values: eighths, quarters, quarter rests and two-beat rests; largest interval a major third (F#4-A4, D4-F#4). Chords D and A (I and V) for the teacher or Band only

Teach in steps: march in place and sing, with hands climbing on "up" and falling on "down"; then let one child play D E F# A up or A F# E D down on bells (or a glockenspiel with only those bars) in bar 3; then a partner answers in bar 6 by copying or going the other way, and the class names which it was. Rotate players each round
dossier.accompaniment: Newly authored, not traditional: D and A chords (I and V). The march style is chosen for a plain parade beat; it is a generic classroom march, not calypso, soca or a steel orchestra, and the classroom bells are not steelpans. dossier.respect: Say steelpan (or pan), not "steel drum"; locate Trinidad and Tobago on a map; say the instrument was invented there by working people and is the national instrument; show a real steel orchestra before classroom instruments imitate brightness. composition.elements: beat and pitch direction (Kindergarten Program 2016) — a sung line that climbs and then falls, a bell player who chooses up or down in the gap after each, and a partner who answers by copying or going the other way
composition.listen: Lord Kitchener — "Pan in 'A' Minor", calypso for the 1987 Trinidad Carnival, heard on Kitchener, Forever Vol. 1 (Charlie's Records / VPAL Music, 2009) via the auto-generated Lord Kitchener channel
composition.bridge: Listen for the bright family of steelpan tone colours and the way a calypso can celebrate the instrument and its players.
composition.context: Steelpan was created in Trinidad and Tobago in the mid-twentieth century, when players in Port of Spain's neighbourhoods turned oil drums into tuned instruments, and grew through community steel orchestras and the Panorama competition. Lord Kitchener (Aldwyn Roberts, 1922-2000) wrote many calypsos about pan that steel orchestras chose for Panorama, "Pan in 'A' Minor" among them in 1987. This original classroom parade song uses voices and barred instruments; it is not calypso and not a steelband score.

Bar 1 G4 G4 quarters; bar 2 A4 A4 eighths, G4 quarter; bar 3 E4 E4 G4 G4 eighths; bar 4 A4 quarter, quarter rest; bar 5 A4 A4 G4 G4 eighths; bar 6 E4 E4 eighths, D4 quarter; bar 7 rest; bar 8 E4 E4 eighths, G4 quarter. dossier.function: original SK partner movement song; partners step on the beat side to side, turn and freeze in a chosen shape, then one shows a new step and the other answers it in the silent bar before the roles swap on "now you lead!"
dossier.elements: eight bars in 2/4 (L:1/8), G major pentatonic, pitch set D-E-G-A (low so, low la, do, re), written range D4-A4 (a perfect fifth). Bars 1-2 "Step, step, side to side" G4 G4 quarters, A4 A4 eighths and G4 quarter; bar 3 "turn a-round and" E4 E4 G4 G4 eighths; bar 4 "stop!" A4 quarter and a quarter rest for the freeze; bar 5 "Show your part-ner" A4 A4 G4 G4; bar 6 "one new step" E4 E4 eighths, D4 quarter; bar 7 a silent bar for the partner's answer; bar 8 "now you lead!" E4 E4 eighths, G4 quarter on the tonic. Form: two four-bar phrases, the first ending open on A4 (re) for the freeze, the second answering down to D4 and home to G4. Note values: eighths, quarters, a quarter rest and one two-beat rest; largest interval a minor third (E4-G4). Chords G, D and C (I, V, IV) for the teacher or Band only
dossier.practice: Start at quarter = 84 and reach the written 96 once partners answer inside bar 7. Rehearsal key G major; the written range D4-A4 is the SK comfort zone and inside the young-unison C4-D5 range. Teach in steps: sing while stepping side to side on the beat; add the turn and the freeze, choosing tall or small; then pair children facing each other, one shows a step in bars 5-6 and the partner answers in bar 7 (mirror, smaller, or the other way); swap on "now you lead!" and repeat. Seated children step with hands or shoulders; keep turns slow and space wide
dossier.accompaniment: Newly authored, not traditional: G, D and C chords (I, V, IV). The pop style gives a generic classroom groove; it is not mbaqanga, kwela, marabi or any South African style, does not copy the "Pata Pata" bass or guitar parts, and must not be labelled as South African music

One syllable per note, stresses on the beats ("STEP, STEP", "SIDE to SIDE", "TURN a-ROUND", "STOP", "SHOW your PART-ner", "ONE new STEP", "NOW you LEAD"); sung. Movement words may be swapped for accessible alternatives; record those as classroom adaptations

It is not traditional, not collected from a community and not modelled on "Pata Pata"; Makeba's recording is a listening bridge only

composition.elements: steady beat, movement direction and partner response (Kindergarten Program 2016) — step on the beat, side to side and turning, freeze in a chosen shape, then show a partner a new step that the partner answers in the silent bar by mirroring, shrinking or turning it
composition.listen: Miriam Makeba — "Pata Pata" (stereo version), the 1967 Reprise single and title track of the album Pata Pata (1967), heard via the auto-generated Miriam Makeba channel from Strut Records' 2019 release
composition.bridge: Hear how repeated vocal and instrumental ideas make social movement feel communal; notice the leader's voice and the group's answer.
composition.context: Miriam Makeba (1932-2008), a South African singer from Johannesburg, first recorded "Pata Pata" in South Africa in 1957; the song, sung partly in isiXhosa, names a township social dance ("pata pata", touch touch), and her 1967 US recording became an international hit. Banned from returning home in 1960 for speaking against apartheid, she lived in exile until 1990. Writing credits differ between sources (Makeba and Jerry Ragovoy on the 1967 release; some histories link the earlier song to Dorothy Masuka). This is a new movement song, not a "Pata Pata" arrangement.

items.title: Rāna jīnāk
items.subtitle: We have come to you: the Maghreb's opening song
items.source: Jules Rouanet, "La musique arabe dans le Maghreb", Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (1922), p. 2824

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (1922), p. 2824 (Rouanet, "La musique arabe dans le Maghreb")
the page before (p. 2823): the festival procession and its instruments

performanceNotes: No recording found yet. Places to look: the Arab Music Archiving and Research foundation (AMAR); the 78s of Edmond Yafil's Algiers label on Gallica (gallica.bnf.fr); Algerian ʿaroubi and ḥawzi singers, who still open feasts with it. Listen before linking.
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Rouanet p. 2824 (the sixteenth run in bar 8, the second ending of the phrase in bar 15, and the accompaniment rhythm). An Arabic speaker who knows Algerian song (darja) to write the opening couplet in Arabic script and check the transliteration and meaning; Rouanet prints only the first words. Classroom check: as a hello song paired with B'qāw ʿala khēr (the goodbye song, its own record).
items.notes: THE PLATE: "Allegro", 2/4, no key signature, three staves with a repeat; words "Ra-na dji-nak, Ya dou-aï-ni, Ra-na dji-nak, Na-ri! Ya na-ri!" Below, "Rythme d'accompagnement": two lines of strokes, the upper (high) and lower (low), "etc."
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with Rouanet's transliterated opening words and their English meaning in an N: line; bar 8's last sixteenth and the place of "Ya" in bar 15 kept as read and named as guessed; equal temperament (no documented tuning); persian style under the record's band lines; keep correcting here

dossier.function: The opening song of the Maghreb feast. Rouanet: "perhaps the best-known tune of the Maghreb"; it is played at religious and secular feasts alike, births, circumcisions, weddings, and the procession to a saint's tomb, and when the procession arrives the ghaitas play it again. The words greet the hosts: "We have come to you!", then wishes of joy and prosperity, the lines broken by the cry "My fire! O my fire!" (Rouanet's footnote 1).
dossier.elements: 2/4, Allegro; eighteen bars sung twice; final A, range G to e (a ninth); a dotted quarter and a sixteenth-note triplet that open each half, a run of eight sixteenths on "ni", and the answering cry "Na-ri! Ya na-ri!".
dossier.practice: Processional and festive: everyone knows it; the shawms (ghaita) and drums play it outdoors at the head of the procession; at home the women's ensemble plays it. In class: a hello song at the start of a lesson, sung as everyone arrives, with B'qāw at the end.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition (Rouanet pp. 2823-2824, 2838): outdoors ghaita (shawm) with tbal (large two-headed drum) and naqqarat (small paired kettledrums); indoors the women's ensemble (messemaʿ) with kamanja (violin), tar (frame drum with jingles) and derbouka (goblet drum). Rouanet prints the "rythme d'accompagnement" under the tune: two strokes, high and low, in 2/4: high on sixteenths 1, 3, 5 and 8 (the 8th is the pickup he begins with), low on 1 and 5. Band here: high stroke on rim, low on bd, exactly his rhythm; no bass or chords (the music is unison, not harmonised). Needs: ghaita (GM shanai), tbal, naqqarat, derbouka.
dossier.lyrics: Rouanet prints only the opening words, "Rana djinak, ya dou aïni ... Nari! Ya nari!": tentatively رانا جيناك يا ضو عيني ... ناري يا ناري, "We have come to you, light of my eyes ... My fire! O my fire!" The rest of each couplet is improvised good wishes (footnote 1). Fit for class. The full couplet, and the Arabic script above, wait for an Arabic speaker (see review).
dossier.honesty: Traditional, anonymous; the notes, the words as far as printed, and the drum rhythm are Rouanet's transcription (1920). The band plays his rhythm on stand-in sounds.
dossier.licence: Jules Rouanet (1858-1944), "La musique arabe dans le Maghreb", in Lavignac and La Laurencie (eds.), Encyclopédie de la musique et dictionnaire du Conservatoire, Part I vol. 5 (Paris: Delagrave, 1922; the section dated "Copyright by Librairie Delagrave, 1920"): public domain in the US (published before 1931) and in Canada (Rouanet d. 1944).
dossier.respect: The tune also leads processions to saints' tombs, where the first verse of the Qur'an is recited aloud (Rouanet p. 2824); the song itself is not a religious text. Rouanet writes as a French colonial musicologist in Algiers; the record quotes his facts about the music, not his framing.
dossier.review: An Arabic speaker familiar with Algerian song, for the words; ideally an Algerian musician, for the tempo and the drum strokes.

items.title: Resvelons nous

items.blocked: Source check: hear all three voices against Stainer pp. 132-133 (IMSLP #344705, pdf pp. 170-171), especially the editorial accidentals (Stainer's sharps and flats over the notes) and the burden's last three bars, which leave the canon. Then classroom check: can a class hold the burden as a two-part round, an octave up, while the teacher sings the top line?
items.notes: THE WORDS (top voice): "Resvelons nous, resvelons, amoureux; / Alons au bois tantost en cilir le may. / Et chanterons chascun un virelay / Pour sa dame: s'en serons plus joieux." Wake up, wake up, lovers; let us go to the woods now to gather the may, and each of us will sing a virelai for his lady, and be the happier for it. The burden: "Alons ent bien tos au may", let's be off to the may.
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 as Stainer reads it (his editorial accidentals kept and said so), with no tuning; keep correcting here

dossier.function: A May-morning song: wake up, lovers, and go to the woods to gather the may (green boughs and blossom brought home on May Day). The burden underneath is the company's own call, "Alons ent bien tos au may", let's be off to the may.
dossier.elements: A five-bar burden sung as a canon: the contratenor sings it, the tenor answers a fifth lower one bar later, each resting a bar before going round again. Over it a solo top line in 3/2. Cadences on D with the open fifth D-A.
dossier.practice: Two groups sing the burden as a round, the second group starting one bar after the first (an octave up for children's voices); a soloist or the teacher sings the top line. The burden alone is a first canon: seven notes, stepwise, a five-bar loop. The band rests; the three voices are the whole piece.
dossier.honesty: Composed, not traditional: Guillaume Du Fay, before about 1436 (the date by which it was copied into Oxford, Bodleian Library, Canonici misc. 213). The notes are Stainer's 1898 transcription, note values halved, with his editorial accidentals.
dossier.licence: Stainer, Dufay and his Contemporaries (London: Novello, 1898): public domain in the US (published 1898) and in Canada (the editors died 1901, 1937 and 1939). Notes read from the IMSLP scan of the Sibley Music Library copy.
dossier.respect: A secular spring song; nothing sacred or sensitive.
dossier.review: An early-music singer or choir director, for the editorial accidentals and the tempo.
dossier.accompaniment: None: the three voices are the whole piece, and the band rests. Style ballad only as a nominal setting, since the band lines silence it (conservative guess, 11 November 2026)
dossier.lyrics: Middle French; the top voice's four lines and the burden, as Stainer underlays them, with an English meaning. Fit for class (conservative guess, 11 November 2026)

items.title: Senufo balafon and djembe (record)
items.subtitle: Two balafons, djembe and shaker in procession: pulse only
items.source: Clip 14 of a Dust-to-Digital Instagram post (19 October 2026), via the Facebook page LA CULTURE SÉNOUFO; pulse read from the recording

sourceUrls.label: Dust-to-Digital on Instagram (posted 19 October 2026), clip 14 of 20: a traditional Senufo performance in West Africa, via LA CULTURE SÉNOUFO on Facebook

performances.label: a Senufo balafon and djembe group in procession (Dust-to-Digital, October 2026, via LA CULTURE SÉNOUFO on Facebook)

performanceNotes: The clip is 26 seconds, filmed in a crowd. For clearer Senufo balafon music: the Facebook page LA CULTURE SÉNOUFO; commercial recordings of Senufo balafon groups from Korhogo (Côte d'Ivoire) and Sikasso (Mali); anthropological studies of the Senufo (Till Förster's, for one) name villages and occasions.
items.blocked: Transcription: the balafon's tuning is measured (an equal five-note scale, below), but its lines could not be read from this clip (two balafons, djembe, shaker and a crowd, filmed on a phone while walking): the strokes found do not settle into a repeating pattern. Find a cleaner recording of a Senufo balafon ensemble, or a printed transcription, before writing any notes. Source check: which village or group, and what the occasion was (the video shows a crowd in green and yellow, likely a festival or a funeral procession).
items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): onsets were detected in the whole clip and folded onto the cycle that repeats best (2.07 s, one 4/4 bar at about 116 beats a minute); every eighth carries a stroke, and no accent pattern stood out of the crowd noise. The balafon keys could not be separated from the drums and crowd (the pitch tracker spread its notes over two octaves with no stable set).
items.kindNote: A record of what the clip holds: the pulse and the balafon's tuning; missing: the balafon parts (the lead's melody and the second's ostinato), the djembe and shaker rhythms, the chanting, and the occasion.

dossier.function: Processional music in a crowd: two balafons carried on the players (the frame is slung so they play while walking), a djembe and a shaker, with people singing and chanting along. Senufo balafon ensembles play at funerals, harvest festivals and initiation celebrations; which this is, the clip does not say.
dossier.elements: Balafons (wooden keys over gourd resonators, with buzzing membranes) tuned to an equal pentatonic: five steps of about 240 cents to the octave, not the Western pentatonic of whole tones and minor thirds; in interlocking lines over a steady eighth-note pulse; the djembe keeps the eighths.
dossier.practice: A steady pulse at about 116 beats a minute (eighths about 0.26 s apart), with a two-second cycle (one 4/4 bar) heard in the djembe. Loud and outdoors; the balafon players move with the crowd.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: two or three balafons (a lead and one or two seconds), djembe or other drums, shaker, and voices. In class: a pentatonic xylophone ostinato over a hand-drum pulse would be the substitute, once the parts are known.
dossier.lyrics: Not taken: the chanting is under the instruments and not clear; any words would be in a Senufo language (Senari or another), to be checked by a speaker.
dossier.honesty: Traditional practice; nothing of the music is transcribed here, only the pulse and the instruments seen and heard.
dossier.licence: The music is traditional; the recording belongs to the performers and the Facebook page that posted it. Nothing was taken but the pulse; no audio or video is kept here.
dossier.respect: If this is a funeral procession, the music belongs to that occasion; find out before teaching any of it as a dance or party piece. Some Senufo balafon music is tied to the Poro society; ask a Senufo musician which pieces may be played outside.
dossier.review: A Senufo balafon player, for the parts and their occasion.

items.title: Si me dan pasteles
items.subtitle: Aguinaldo: Puerto Rican Christmas song in two voices
items.source: Allena Luce, Canciones populares (New York: Silver, Burdett, 1921), "Aguinaldo (Si me dan pasteles)", p. 3

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Allena Luce, Canciones populares (1921), p. 3

performances.label: Library of Congress Folklife blog on Sidney Robertson Cowell's recordings, including Aurora Calderón singing this aguinaldo in Oakland, 10 April 1939 (LOC item 2017700903)
Los Borincanos (title checked, not yet listened to)
Los Aguadillanos (title checked, not yet listened to)

performanceNotes: The instrument line-up for aguinaldos is documented on Folkways FW 8802, Songs and Dances of Puerto Rico (recorded by William S. Marlens, 1956): Cuarteto Puerto Rico of Cayey on cuatro, tres, maracas, claves, güiro and bongó (liner notes at folkways-media.si.edu/docs/folkways/artwork/FW08802.pdf).
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Luce p. 3, especially bar 7 (the lower voice reads G under c, c, B, c: a fourth, not a third) and the last bar (one chord, d over F sharp, under the two syllables "gen-te"). Also the ritornello (transcribed 2026-11-11): its bars 4 and 8 (sixteenths and the staccato run) and the second ending's chord (F sharp, c, d: a D7 into the verse). Listen to the 1939 Library of Congress recording before trusting the band's güiro and maracas. A Spanish-speaking (Puerto Rican) teacher for the words and the parranda.
items.notes: THE PLATE: G minor, 2/4; an instrumental ritornello (two systems, Fine at the first ending), then the sung verse with a repeat, its melody doubled in thirds in the pianist's right hand, the words above; Luce's preface: collected from students of the University of Puerto Rico, versions chosen by their vote.
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with the record's readings of the ritornello's bar 8, the verse's bar 7 lower voice and the last bar's "gen-te" on one chord marked as guesses, and the words added under Voice 2; keep correcting here

dossier.function: A Christmas aguinaldo: at Christmas, groups of singers and players go from house to house (the parranda), and the hosts give them a little gift or refreshments; the song's frank hint is that the visitors expect pasteles, and hot ones (Luce's note).
dossier.elements: G minor, 2/4, eight bars sung twice; the melody in parallel thirds with a second voice beneath; each line a quick run of eighths and a held note ("pas-te-les__", "ca-lien-tes__"); range of the top voice A to d.
dossier.practice: Sung by the visiting group, two voices in thirds, with the players' ritornello between verses, and verses made up on the spot (Luce mentions many amusing variants). In class: half the room on the melody, half on the third below; then make up a verse for the class's own party food.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition (FW 8802 notes): cuatro (the ten-string Puerto Rican guitar) and tres strum and play the ritornello; güiro (scraped gourd), maracas, claves and bongó keep the beat. Band here: the cabasa as a güiro stand-in, long scrape then two short (a common güiro figure; ours, to be checked against the recordings), shakers for the maracas, the nylon guitar strumming the chords the band finds, and the bass. Needs: güiro, cuatro, bongó (the drum-sample work in progress may cover the percussion).
dossier.lyrics: Spanish: "Si me dan pasteles, dénmelos calientes, que pasteles fríos empachan la gente": "If you give me pasteles, give them to me hot, for cold pasteles give people a stomach-ache." A variant Luce quotes: "Denme mi aguinaldo, si me lo han de dar, que la noche es corta y tenemos que andar": "Give me my aguinaldo, if you're going to give it, for the night is short and we have far to go." Pasteles are Puerto Rican Christmas parcels of mashed plantain and root vegetables with a filling, wrapped in banana leaves. Fit for class.
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the two sung voices as Luce printed them (top two notes of her right hand where it has three), not her piano part. The güiro, maracas and the band's chords are ours, after the documented line-up.
dossier.licence: Allena Luce (compiler), Canciones populares (New York: Silver, Burdett, copyright 1921): public domain in the US (published 1921). Luce's death year is not known, so the Canadian status is unconfirmed; the record takes only the traditional tune and its thirds, not her arrangement.
dossier.respect: A seasonal Christian custom with secular words; fine for a winter-holiday unit that includes other traditions. Nothing sensitive.
dossier.review: A Puerto Rican teacher or musician, for the words, the parranda and the cuatro's part.

items.title: Đàn đá (S'tiêng lithophone)
items.subtitle: A girl playing the lithophone at home in Bình Phước, as heard in the clip
items.source: Clip 17 of a Dust-to-Digital Instagram post (19 October 2026), via the player's Facebook page; draft transcription by machine, from the recording

sourceUrls.label: Dust-to-Digital on Instagram (posted 19 October 2026), clip 17 of 20: "XTiêng Đn Xinh" playing a lithophone at her home in Bình Phước, Vietnam, via her Facebook page

performances.label: a girl playing the đàn đá (lithophone) at home in Bình Phước (Dust-to-Digital, October 2026, via her Facebook page)

performanceNotes: The clip is 60 seconds of one piece, indoors. For the instrument: the S'tiêng and M'nông lithophones of Bình Phước and Đắk Nông, the first described in the West being the Ndut Lieng Krak lithophone that Georges Condominas found in 1949 (now in Paris); the Vietnamese Institute of Musicology (Hà Nội) holds field recordings.
items.blocked: Source check: which piece she plays (it may be a traditional S'tiêng melody or a Vietnamese song by a named composer; many đàn đá players play both), and the player's name, which the caption gives only as "XTiêng Đn Xinh" with letters lost; until the piece is named, nothing here is used in class. Transcription: the whole minute is drafted below (intro, the tune twice, a high closing section); check it by ear against the clip, especially the high B (b'), which may be an overtone of the F sharp stone where the two sound together.
items.notes: HOW READ (2026-11-11): the clip's sustained part (harmonic/percussive separation) was factored into 18 spectra; 13 were single stones (C sharp 5, E5, F sharp 5, G sharp 5, A5, B5, C sharp 6, D6, E6, F sharp 6, a stone near B6) or their upper partials (the components at C7, D7, E7, F7 and A sharp 6 rise and fall with A5, C sharp 6, B5, C sharp 5 and F sharp 5, and are read as those stones), and three were noise. Strokes were found by spectral flux in the full mix and set on a 0.441 s beat from 0.36 s; the tune's two passes (12.5 s and 28.6 s) agree in 45 of their 56 eighths, bars 2 to 4 exactly; they differ in the first bar (the second pass starts an eighth later) and in the last two (the first leads into the link, the second into the closing section).

dossier.function: Solo playing at home on a đàn đá, a lithophone: a row of long, roughly shaped stone slabs laid on a padded frame (here about ten to fifteen stones on two tiers), struck with two mallets. The girl plays standing, a mallet in each hand.
dossier.elements: Six-note scale on A (A, B, C sharp, E, F sharp, with G sharp as a passing note), from C sharp 5 up to F sharp 6, plus one high stone near B6. Form: a seven-bar intro of broken chords in both hands (C sharp, F sharp, A low; C sharp 6 and G sharp answering), the tune A (seven bars, built on repeated C sharp 6 and E6 falling through B and A to F sharp and E) played twice with a two-bar link of high B and A between, then a closing section that rolls on F sharp 5 and F sharp 6 and settles on C sharp 6 and E6, ending on repeated E6.
dossier.practice: A steady beat of 136 a minute (0.441 s, held through the whole minute), in eighths; the stones ring about half a second, so the notes overlap. One hand mostly carries the tune; the other adds the low F sharp or A under it, or strikes the same stone in alternation for the repeated notes.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: the lithophone alone, or with gongs and drums in the old ensembles. Here the stones alone; the band is off. In class: glockenspiel or metallophone on the six notes, two mallets.
dossier.lyrics: None: instrumental (if the piece turns out to be a song, its words belong in this record).
dossier.honesty: A draft of one performance. The stones were separated by a spectrogram factorization (one learned spectrum per stone), each stroke was assigned to the stone whose sound jumped at that moment, and the strokes were set on an eighth-note grid of 0.2205 s; the two passes of the tune agree almost note for note. The bar lines, the note lengths (every stroke is written to the next one; the stones ring on) and the spelling are ours.
dossier.licence: The instrument and its old repertoire are traditional; the piece is not identified and could be a composed Vietnamese song. The recording belongs to the player; only the notes were taken, and no audio or video is kept here.
dossier.respect: A young player filmed at home and posted on her own page: credit her by name once it is known, and ask before any use beyond study. Lithophones of the Central Highlands and the southeast are a source of local and national pride; present the instrument with its people, the S'tiêng.
dossier.review: The player or her family, for the piece's name; a Vietnamese musicologist who knows the đàn đá of Bình Phước.

items.title: O tu'la, mntwa'na (Thula, mntwana)
items.subtitle: O hush thee, baby: Zulu lullaby
items.source: Natalie Curtis Burlin, Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (New York: G. Schirmer, 1920), "Igama la Bantwana: Song of Children (Lullaby)", p. 135; words and notes pp. 66-68

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Curtis, Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (1920), p. 135 (music)
the same, pp. 66-68: the words with Curtis's literal and metrical translations, and her note

performanceNotes: No recording of this melody found. Curtis made phonograph records of her singers (book p. xxv), not yet located. The modern Zulu lullaby "Thula Mntwana" (taught by Sbongiseni Duma in Carnegie Hall's Musical Explorers) shares the theme, a child waiting for its mother, but is very likely a different tune; listen before comparing. A transcription with a Zulu tradition-bearer (CC0, credited by name) would be the best companion record.
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Curtis p. 135, especially the three glides (Curtis's *1 and *2) and bar 13's first note (*3, "between D sharp and E"). A Zulu speaker to give the modern spelling (Curtis writes "O tu'la, mntwa'na"; today "Thula, mntwana"), check the words and translation, and say whether this tune is still sung. Classroom check: sung softly, swaying, with no accompaniment.
items.notes: CURTIS'S FOOTNOTES (p. 135): *1 "Intervals blurred in a long cooing, downward slur from B to E." *2 "Intervals a little more distinct than in the former phrase, because of the pronounced retard, but all the indeterminate sounds in the downward sweep, from interval to interval, are heard as when the finger slides from stop to stop on the violin." *3 "Note between D sharp and E" (the first note of bar 13, written here as D sharp).
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with bar 13's first note as D sharp (Curtis: between D sharp and E), the glides as the record writes them, Curtis's 1920 spelling, %%style ballad with the band silent, and Curtis's colonial framing kept out, with a one-sentence teacher's note on it; keep correcting here

dossier.function: A Zulu lullaby "very commonly used to put Zulu babies to sleep" (Curtis, from Madikane Cele). A mother has had to cross the mountains and left her baby with another woman, a grandmother, an aunt or a co-wife, who quiets the crying child: your mother is not with you, the zig-zag trail has held her; she is coming soon, she will bring you something pretty (fruit or bright berries).
dossier.elements: 6/8, dotted quarter = 50, "sung softly and with swaying rhythm"; E major, range E to e (an octave); the rocking quarter-eighth figure throughout; three "cooing" glides falling from B to E (Curtis: "intervals blurred in a long cooing, downward slur"), each ending a half-verse on "I-wa!", the last two with a ritardando.
dossier.practice: Sung by one woman to a baby carried on her back, swaying. In class: everyone sings softly and sways on the dotted quarters; the glides are slid, not stepped ("as when the finger slides from stop to stop on the violin", Curtis's footnote).
dossier.accompaniment: None: a lullaby sung to one child, with the swaying of the singer's body as its only beat (Curtis pp. 66-67). Band: rests. A soft shaker on each dotted quarter would be our addition and is not written; the record leaves the voice alone.
dossier.lyrics: Zulu, in Curtis's 1920 spelling, with her metrical translation (which she says matches the Zulu accents and line lengths): "O hush thee, baby, O hush thee! Thy mother is not with thee; she tarried in the mountains, the zig-zag trail hath held her. I-wa! O hush thee, baby, O hush thee! Thy mother soon is coming, she'll bring thee pretty berries. I-wa!" Fit for class. The spelling waits for a Zulu speaker (see review).
dossier.honesty: Traditional; notes, words, glides and tempo as Curtis printed them from Madikane Qandeyana Cele's singing. Nothing added.
dossier.licence: Natalie Curtis Burlin (d. 1921), Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (G. Schirmer, 1920): public domain in the US and in Canada.
dossier.respect: Nothing sacred. Credit Madikane Cele. Curtis's surrounding remarks on race ("naturally emotional", "primitive races", the missionary anecdotes) stay out of the record; her account of the song and its use is kept.
dossier.review: A Zulu speaker, for the spelling, the words and whether the tune is known today.

items.title: Usagi to Kame (兎と亀)

items.source: Florence Hudson Botsford (ed.), Folk Songs of Many Peoples, vol. 2 (New York: The Woman's Press, 1922), "The Rabbit and the Turtle," pp. 442-443, English version by Grace Hazard Conkling; University of Rochester Sibley Music Library, public domain

sourceUrls.label: University of Rochester Sibley Music Library catalogue and public-domain determination for Folk Songs of Many Peoples
stable University of Rochester handle for both volumes
Kunitachi College of Music Library song index naming Wasaburō Ishihara and Benjirō Nōsho and giving the melody incipit
Kanagawa Prefectural Library exhibition guide identifying the 1901-1902 school-song collection and its educational context

performanceNotes: No modern recording was used for the transcription. The 1922 score provides an English dialogue version and Japanese-script text; ask the named reviewer to demonstrate the Japanese words rather than copying a commercial children's recording or its arrangement.
items.blocked: The melody, authorship and 1901 publication history are checked, but no human review has occurred. A Japanese children's-music educator or shōka historian, a competent Japanese speaker, a second score reader, a rights reviewer for the 1922 English version and a classroom music teacher must check the text, translation, dialogue game and teaching frame before publication.
items.notes: CONTEXT: Kunitachi College of Music Library identifies the song as "Usagi to Kame," names Ishihara and Nōsho and gives the incipit. Kanagawa Prefectural Library places it in the graded 1901-1902 Yōnen Shōka collection, written for primary-school children. That evidence supports an authored school-song identity, not the "traditional Japanese folk song" label sometimes attached to it.
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with Conkling's 1922 English stanza only (the Japanese words not yet set), labelled as a 1901 school song by Nōsho and Ishihara; folk style with the record's muted band lines, equal temperament; keep correcting here

dossier.function: Japanese composed children's teaching song retelling the hare-and-tortoise race as dialogue; useful for character roles, quick dotted rhythms, steady 2/4 pulse and comparing boastful and patient delivery
dossier.elements: sixteen two-four bars in C major, repeated dotted-eighth/sixteenth cells, C4-D5 octave-plus-second classroom range, four balanced four-bar phrases and a melody that repeatedly contrasts G-E gestures with held C or G cadences
dossier.practice: The 1922 plate marks Allegro but gives no metronome number; quarter note = 104 is our rehearsal estimate. Assign the first English-source stanza to the rabbit and let the class speak the later turtle answer before deciding whether to sing reviewed Japanese words. C4-D5 exactly spans the conservative young-unison range, and C major is the practical first rehearsal key
dossier.accompaniment: Botsford prints an uncredited piano accompaniment, but this record transcribes only the vocal line. Begin with voice and a walking pulse or alternating knee taps; do not infer koto, shamisen, taiko or a min'yō accompaniment. Any generated chords or percussion must be labelled as our classroom arrangement rather than Japanese traditional practice
dossier.lyrics: Wasaburō Ishihara's Japanese text and Benjirō Nōsho's music first appeared in a 1901 school-song collection. Botsford prints Japanese script on p. 443 and aligns Grace Hazard Conkling's English version to the melody on p. 442. This ABC preserves only that source-aligned English stanza pending Japanese transcription, modern orthography, pronunciation and translation review
dossier.honesty: Authored historical school song, not anonymous warabe-uta: music by Benjirō Nōsho and Japanese words by Wasaburō Ishihara. The melody and English words follow Botsford's 1922 plate; composer/lyricist attribution is independently confirmed by Kunitachi College of Music Library. ABC spelling, bar numbering, rehearsal tempo, melody-only reduction and muted-band directives are ours
dossier.licence: Ishihara died in 1922 and Nōsho in 1936, so the 1901 composition is public domain. University of Rochester marks the complete 1922 source item public domain. Grace Hazard Conkling's English version is reproduced from that institutional PD item, but a rights reviewer must still confirm its status for every launch jurisdiction because Conkling died in 1958
dossier.respect: Present this as a Meiji-period composed school song and fable, not a timeless or generic Japanese folk tune. Do not add costumes, accents or instruments merely from geography. A Japanese reviewer should decide how to explain the school-song movement and whether the historical English adaptation is suitable beside checked Japanese words
dossier.review: Japanese children's-music educator or shōka historian, competent Japanese speaker, rights reviewer for the English version, second score reader and classroom music teacher; all reviews still required

items.title: Vámonos por Santa Anita
items.subtitle: Come, let's go to Santa Anita: Mexican play song
items.source: Eleanor Hague, Spanish-American Folk-Songs, Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society 10 (1917), No. 75, p. 98

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Hague, Spanish-American Folk-Songs (1917), at p. 98

items.blocked: Source check: compare with Hague No. 75, p. 98 (the dotted-eighth and sixteenth figures in every beat). Classroom check: can a class keep the dotted figure long-short, not even, at a gay tempo?
items.notes: THE PLATE: "Gayly", 2/4 in G major, two lines of four bars with the same notes, Spanish words with Hague's English under them: "Come, let's go to Santa Anita! Come, let's go! for there you'll find / In the lead the wagons harnessed, And the oxen on behind."

dossier.function: A light play song from northern Mexico: come, let's go to Santa Anita (a village outing), the oxcarts in front and the oxen behind.
dossier.elements: G major, 2/4, four bars sung twice; every beat but the last is a dotted eighth and a sixteenth, a skipping long-short figure; a range of a ninth (D above middle C to the E an octave higher).
dossier.practice: Gayly (Hague). The skipping figure suits skipping or a walking game in pairs; the second line of words takes the same four bars.
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the notes, Spanish words and English singing translation as Hague printed them from Mrs. Karbe's singing.
dossier.licence: Eleanor Hague (1875-1954), Spanish-American Folk-Songs, Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society 10 (1917): public domain in the US and in Canada (Hague d. 1954).
dossier.respect: A play song; nothing sacred or sensitive.
dossier.review: A Spanish-speaking teacher, for the words.
dossier.accompaniment: The record transcribes the voice alone; no traditional accompaniment is documented here. Band: the folk (boom-chick) style, a light 2/4 accompaniment for a play song (conservative guess, 11 November 2026)
dossier.lyrics: Spanish, two lines sung to the repeated four bars, then Hague's English singing translation. Fit for class (conservative guess, 11 November 2026)

items.title: Xianhua diao (鮮花調)
items.subtitle: The fresh flower: Chinese popular song, two early versions
items.source: J. A. van Aalst, Chinese Music (Shanghai, 1884), p. 19; John Barrow, Travels in China (London, 1804), p. 316, as taken down by J. C. Hüttner

sourceUrls.label: van Aalst, Chinese Music (1884), p. 19: "Song called 鮮花 (The Fresh Beautiful Flower)", staff and gongche
van Aalst p. 16: his table of the gongche note names
Barrow, Travels in China (1804), p. 316: "Moo-lee-wha", with stanza I (stanza II and the literal translation on p. 317)

performances.label: Harvard, Sounding China: the Barrow and Hüttner tune and its early European history (with performances)
Zhang Ye, Jiangsu folk song broadcast: the modern (1957) "Mo li hua", for comparison, not this text or tune exactly (title checked, not yet listened to)

performanceNotes: Wanted: a Jiangsu or Yangzhou xiaodiao singer, or a sizhu ensemble, singing Xianhua diao in the older form; Berthold Laufer's 1901 cylinders from Shanghai (Indiana University Archives of Traditional Music) are the earliest recordings of the region's songs.
items.blocked: Source check: van Aalst p. 19 (staff and gongche agree; check bar 11's last note B and the old-style quarter rests) and Barrow p. 316 (bars 9-11 and 13, and the last bar, printed as a dotted half). A Chinese speaker to confirm the characters behind Barrow's romanization and to fit stanza I to one of the two melodies (neither source prints the words under the notes). Engine: the band wants a heterophony part (the tune itself on a second instrument, ornamented) before this sounds like the tradition.
items.notes: VAN AALST'S GONGCHE (p. 19), read top to bottom, right to left, with his gamut (p. 16: 合 C, 四 D (printed 士), 上 F, 尺 G, 工 A, 凡 B, 六 c, 五 d; dots after a note lengthen it, a circle marks the fourth beat): 工· 工 六 五 凡 凡 五。 六·· 五 六。 (twice) | 工· 六· 六· 五 凡。 六·· 五 六。 工·· 尺 六 工 尺。 上·· 尺 上。 工·· 上· 尺·。 六·· 五 六。 尺·· 工 尺 上 合。 士·· 上·· 尺· 工 士。 六·· 凡 五 六 工 尺。 六···. It agrees with his staff note for note, which settles the staff's two lowest notes (合 C and 士 D).
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with both versions as read, no words under the notes (neither source sets them) and the English sense of Barrow's two stanzas in an N: line; Barrow's short last bar kept with a rest; ballad style under the record's band lines, equal temperament; keep correcting here

dossier.function: A popular song (xiaodiao) of the lower Yangzi, sung for entertainment by a solo singer who often accompanied herself or himself; Barrow heard it in Canton and calls it "one of the most popular songs in the whole country"; van Aalst prints it as a popular song a century later. Its words praise a fresh flower, the jasmine (moli), too lovely to pick.
dossier.elements: Pentatonic (F G A c d in van Aalst, the gong mode on F with B natural, 凡, as a passing tone; G A B d e in Barrow, the gong mode on G), both ending on the fifth degree (zhi); 4/4 in eighths and quarters with a dotted quarter at each half-line; van Aalst C to d (a ninth), Barrow D to g (an eleventh).
dossier.practice: Sung solo, unhurried, the singer ornamenting the line; the instruments play the same tune together, each a little differently (heterophony), never in chords (Barrow p. 315; van Aalst p. 36). In class: sing or play van Aalst's version (smaller range) on the recorder; then hear Barrow's and find what changed.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: Barrow (p. 315) heard the singer accompany himself "with a kind of guitar" (a pipa or sanxian); Chinese bands play "in unison, and sometimes an instrument takes the octave", never in parts. Van Aalst (p. 36): the popular band is two pipa (played by girls who also sing), sanxian, one or two fiddles (erhu, huqin), a small drum beating time, flute (dizi) and yangqin, all on the melody. Band here: only a clapper (wood block) on the first beat of each bar, standing in for the ban or small drum; no bass, no chords, because the music has none. Needs: a heterophony part (the tune on a second sound with ornaments), and dizi, erhu, pipa, yangqin sounds; until then, a teacher can play the tune on the recorder with the class singing.
dossier.lyrics: Barrow prints two stanzas in 1790s romanization with a word-by-word translation (p. 317). Our reading of the characters (tentative, for a Chinese speaker to confirm): I. 好一朵鮮花，有朝一日落在我家，我本待不出門，對着鮮花兒樂。 "How delightful this branch of fresh flowers! One morning it fell into my house. I, the owner, will not go out; I will sit with the fresh flower and be happy." II. 好一朵茉莉花，滿園花開賽不過它，我本待採一朵戴，又恐看花人兒罵。 "How delightful this jasmine flower! In the full garden no flower excels it. I would pick one to wear, but fear the flower's keeper would scold." Both fit for class. Not underlaid: neither source sets the words to the notes. Not the 1957 He Fang text and tune ("好一朵美丽的茉莉花"), which is in copyright.
dossier.honesty: Traditional. Van Aalst's version as he printed it in staff notation and gongche (they agree); Barrow's as Johann Christian Hüttner took it down "in its unadorned state". The clapper on the downbeat is ours.
dossier.licence: J. A. van Aalst (1858-after 1914), Chinese Music (Shanghai: Inspectorate General of Customs, 1884); John Barrow (1764-1848), Travels in China (London: Cadell and Davies, 1804), tune taken down by Hüttner (d. 1847): both public domain in the US and Canada.
dossier.respect: Barrow and van Aalst write as outsiders who often dismiss Chinese music (Barrow's "aggregation of harsh sounds"); the record keeps their facts and transcriptions only. The tune became a political symbol in 2011 (the "Jasmine Revolution" calls); not something to raise in class unless asked.
dossier.review: A Chinese speaker for the characters and the singing; ideally a musician who plays Jiangnan sizhu, for the ornaments.

items.title: Zdravets
items.subtitle: Geranium: Bulgarian horo song in 9/16
items.source: Vasil Stoin, Narodna pesnopoyka (Sofia, 1930), No. 102 "Zdravets", p. 98

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Stoin, Narodna pesnopoyka (1930), at p. 98, No. 102

performances.label: CREM-CNRS catalogue entry for the Serbian variant (metadata only)

performanceNotes: No recording of this Bulgarian song was found. A Serbian variant, "Zdravche, venche, beru li te mome?" (Orljane, Serbia, recorded by Radmila Petrović, Radio Belgrade 1981), is in the CREM-CNRS archive (CNRSMH_E_1988_011_001_014), listening restricted. The Bulgarian National Radio folklore archive is the place to ask for a Bulgarian one.
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Stoin No. 102, p. 98 (bar 3 of each line, the slurs, and the repeat marks at the line ends). A Bulgarian speaker to check the modern spelling, the stresses and the translation. Classroom check: count 9 as 2+2+2+3 with Stoin's syllables, then dance a simple horo step to it.
items.notes: THE WORDS (Stoin, modern spelling): "Здравче, венче, берат ли те моми?" / "Та мене ли моми да не берат? / Като цъфтя, все гора мирише. / Като дойде на ден на Гергьовден, / те си дойдат хубави девойки, / та ме берат във нови цедила, / та ме носят на бързи потоци, / та ме вият на зелени венци / и ме турят на вакли агънца."
items.decisionNote: published to main on 11 November 2026 with the second note of bar 3 in each line (c) marked as a guess and the transliteration and English as text; keep correcting here

dossier.function: A horo song: sung while dancing the horo, the line dance of Bulgarian village festivities. A question and its answer: "Little geranium, little wreath, do the girls pick you?" and the geranium tells how the girls pick it on St George's Day, weave it into wreaths and crown the lambs. Zdravets (Geranium macrorrhizum) carries the word for health, zdrave, and is given for health at feasts.
dossier.elements: 9/16 in the grouping 2+2+2+3 (quick-quick-quick-slow), the daychovo horo's metre; two three-bar lines, each a ten-syllable verse line; final A with B flat above it, a range of a sixth (F to d).
dossier.practice: Fast (Stoin: Бързо). Horo songs were sung by two groups of women, one at each end of the dance line, answering each other line by line; instruments came in after the singing. In class, two halves of the room take alternate lines while the rest step the horo: count "1 2 3 4-a" (Stoin's pp. 243-245 count uneven metres with syllables).
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: the horo is first sung unaccompanied by the two groups (see practice); played horos use gaida (bagpipe with a drone), kaval (rim-blown flute), gadulka (bowed fiddle), tambura (long-necked lute) and tapan (two-headed drum, a heavy beater on one head and a thin switch on the other). Sources: Stoin's heading "Пѣе се на хоро" (sung at the horo); for the instruments and the singing groups, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Bulgaria (to be replaced by an ethnography). Band here: the tapan only, the heavy beater (bd) on the first beat and the switch (rim) on the other three, one bar of 2+2+2+3; and a held A on the bass as a stand-in for the gaida's drone. Needs: tapan, gaida (GM bagpipe), kaval, gadulka.
dossier.lyrics: All of Stoin's words are fit for class: the question, then eight lines of answer, sung two lines to each pass of the tune (five passes). Written here in modern Bulgarian spelling (Stoin uses the pre-1945 spelling: вѣнче, бератъ), with a transliteration and our English translation; to be checked by a Bulgarian speaker. "Вакли агънца" are lambs with dark rings round the eyes.
dossier.honesty: Traditional, no composer named (Stoin's book also has composed school songs; No. 102 is not one of them). Notes and words as Stoin printed them. The tapan pattern and the drone are ours, after the practice described above; turn the band off to hear the song as the singers sang it.
dossier.licence: Vasil Stoin (1880-1938), Narodna pesnopoyka (Sofia: Ministry of Education, 1930): public domain in the US (published 1930; PD from 1 January 2026) and in Canada and Bulgaria (Stoin d. 1938).
dossier.respect: St George's Day (Gergyovden, 6 May) is a Christian and folk feast; the garlanded lamb is the feast's sacrificed lamb (kurban). That is a fact a teacher may give or leave; the song itself is about flowers, girls and lambs.
dossier.review: A Bulgarian speaker, for the spelling, stresses and translation; a Bulgarian dance teacher, for the horo step.
